articles.title: IND vs NZ 4th ODI | 'Pace is good, but skills matter': Auqib Nabi on adapting to New Zealand conditions
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India pacer Auqib Nabi believes that having pace is an advantage, but trusting one's skills is equally important.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India pacer Auqib Nabi believes that having pace is an advantage, but trusting one's skills is equally important. The Jammu and Kashmir pacer says he will stick to the methods that brought him success in domestic cricket as he prepares for the fourth ODI against New Zealand.Nabi had a quiet start to the five-match series, returning figures of 0/33 in the first ODI, which India won by five wickets (DLS method).He bounced back in the second match, dismissing New Zealand openers Will Young and Tim Seifert to help India register a four-run victory (DLS method).The third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned due to rain, with India leading the series 2-0. The fourth match will be played at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday."Having pace is good but I back my skills. I will do what I have been doing and what has brought me here. I will just do what I did in domestic cricket, and that will help me here too," Nabi said during the press conference ahead of the fourth ODI.Learning to bowl in New Zealand conditionsPlaying his first series in New Zealand, Nabi knows that he will need to adapt to the conditions. The pacer believes that seam movement will be important, as batters can deal with swing bowling."It is my first time in New Zealand. You need to rely more on seam here. Use scrambled seam because swing can be dealt with," he said.Nabi also highlighted the importance of bowling with discipline, particularly on good batting pitches where bowlers can easily leak runs."You need to bowl well no matter how good or flat the pitches are. When wickets are good, you need to bowl with discipline because you can go for runs," he said."We keep discussing amongst ourselves about plans for drop-in pitches. With Arshdeep and Anshul both," he said."Weather back home and here is similar. Opposition and level of cricket is different," he said.From Ranji Trophy success to India coloursKnown as the 'Baramulla Express', Nabi earned his place in the Indian team through consistent performances in domestic cricket.The Jammu and Kashmir pacer picked up 104 wickets across the 2024-25 and 2025-26 Ranji Trophy seasons. His standout performance came in the 2025-26 season, when he picked 60 wickets in 17 innings at an average of 12.65. His efforts played a key role in Jammu and Kashmir winning their maiden Ranji Trophy title. He was also named Player of the Tournament.Nabi admitted that he had expected a Test call-up before getting an opportunity in white-ball cricket. However, he believes the current experience will help him when he gets another chance in the red-ball format."I was expecting a red-ball call-up before white-ball cricket, but this experience will also be very helpful. And then also staying with the Test team," he said."Very happy to play for India. Khelna India ke liye bahut badi baat hai. Mera bhi wohi tha," he added."Whenever people say about facilities, I always say do your best and things will fall in place," the pacer said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IPL: Hardik Pandya, Arshdeep Singh swap jerseys
articles.summary: MUMBAI: In one of the biggest trades in IPL history, Mumbai Indians (MI) and Punjab Kings (PBKS) have swapped two of India's premier white-ball players,
articles.body: MUMBAI: In one of the biggest trades in IPL history, Mumbai Indians (MI) and Punjab Kings (PBKS) have swapped two of India's premier white-ball players, with Hardik Pandya moving to Punjab and Arshdeep Singh heading to Mumbai.Pandya, who captained MI over the last three seasons but could not restore the franchise to its title-winning ways, will begin a new chapter with PBKS. The IPL confirmed on Wednesday that Pandya will join Punjab for Rs 18 crore, up from his previous fee of Rs 16.35 crore, while Arshdeep moves to MI on his existing Rs 18-crore contract.Pandya had attracted interest from multiple franchises, with Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals understood to have explored a deal. However, PBKS succeeded in landing the India all-rounder by parting with their premier fast bowler in what is arguably the most significant trade ahead of the league's 20th edition.The move reflects the differing priorities of the two franchises. Punjab, still chasing their maiden IPL title, have acquired an experienced match-winner and proven leader, while MI have secured one of the world's best left-arm pacers to bolster their bowling attack.While Pandya has harboured captaincy ambitions at the international level and franchise level, he swiftly put to rest any speculation over Punjab's leadership structure, making it clear that he would play under captain Shreyas Iyer. Posting a picture in PBKS colours on Instagram, he wrote: "Sat Sri Akal. My captain, Shreyas. My coach, Ricky. My team, all of Punjab. I am standing behind you."For MI, Arshdeep's arrival fills a long-standing gap. Partnering Jasprit Bumrah, India's talismanic fast bowler now has an equally accomplished left-arm counterpart alongside him. Arshdeep's ability to swing the new ball and execute yorkers at the death gives Mumbai a varied and potent pace attack.Arshdeep leaves PBKS after eight seasons with the franchise, during which he became their highest wicket-taker with 111 wickets in 96 matches. His IPL exploits paved the way for international success, and he currently stands as India's leading wicket-taker in T20Is with 151 wickets in 104 matches."Arshdeep's arrival adds an exciting dimension to our bowling attack," MI owner Akash Ambani said. "He brings the right blend of experience, skill and hunger to compete."Punjab, meanwhile, paid an emotional tribute to their departing stalwart, posting on social media: "From a young sher to a name that made Punjab proud. You'll always have a home here, Arsh paa."The trade also brings the curtain down on Pandya's eventful association with MI. He was a key member of their title-winning sides in 2015, 2017, 2019 and 2020 before leading Gujarat Titans to the IPL crown in 2022 and another final in 2023. He returned to Mumbai as captain in 2024, replacing Rohit Sharma, but endured mixed fortunes.Under Pandya, MI finished last in 2024, reached the playoffs in 2025 and ended ninth in 2026. His record as captain read 15 wins and 24 defeats in 39 matches."Hardik has shared some very special moments with MI," Ambani said. "We have seen him grow as a cricketer, make his mark on the world stage and then return to lead the team. We wish him nothing but the very best."TOI understands that PBKS skipper Iyer played a significant role in convincing Pandya to make the move. While Punjab gain a proven all-rounder, a power hitter and finisher and leadership option, MI embark on a new era under head coach Kieron Pollard, with Robin Uthappa, Mitchell McClenaghan and T Dilip joining the support staff ahead of IPL 2027.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'We absolutely support Pat': Cricket Australia backs Cummins amid fresh Sandpapergate row
articles.summary: Cricket Australia chairman David Boon has thrown his support behind Test captain Pat Cummins following fresh allegations about the 2018 ball-tampering
articles.body: Cricket Australia chairman David Boon has thrown his support behind Test captain Pat Cummins following fresh allegations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. Boon has made it clear that Cummins' position as captain is safe and that the board continues to have full faith in him.The controversy has returned to the spotlight after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja made fresh claims in his autobiography, "Sabr". Khawaja alleged that all members of the Australian team on the 2018 South Africa tour knew about the plan to tamper with the ball.His claims have reopened the debate over the scandal and led to demands for another investigation. Cummins, who now leads Australia's Test team, has also come under pressure to explain what he knew.Boon says Cricket Australia has full faith in CumminsBoon said Cummins had led the team with honesty and had the board's complete backing.“We absolutely support Pat,” Boon said in comments published by The Australian on Thursday.“He’s been an exemplary captain, he’s led the team with integrity and, you know, very successfully over the period of time that he’s been captain, so there’s no question of our confidence in him continuing on in that fact.”Cummins has not yet publicly addressed Khawaja's allegations. He, however, posted on X that he would speak to the media on Friday after going through the claims."I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly," he wrote.Mitchell Marsh, Australia's white-ball captain, is also expected to address the issue. Marsh was part of the Test team during the 2018 tour and will speak at a press conference in Perth later on Thursday, ahead of the ODI against England.Warner and Sayers support Khawaja's versionKhawaja's claims have received support from former teammate David Warner. Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were all banned for their roles in the ball-tampering scandal.Former Australia fast bowler Chadd Sayers, who was also part of the 2018 South Africa tour, has also backed Khawaja. Speaking to Australian media last weekend, Sayers said the allegations were "accurate".Despite the fresh claims, Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg said on Tuesday that there was no compelling reason to reopen the investigation.Boon repeated the same position, saying the board did not want to get into a dispute over different versions of events."I respect (Usman’s) point of view and his recollections of what occurred, and they’re his, but we don’t want to get into a he-said-she-said argument," he said."There are going to be supporters, there’s going to be other guys that don’t recollect the same thing, so I don’t see a purpose.”Hick and Starc deny prior knowledgeIn his book "Sabr", released this week, Khawaja claimed that Australia had tampered with the ball during the second Test in South Africa as well, and not just in the third Test in Cape Town.Former Australia batting coach Graeme Hick has strongly rejected the claims, calling them "absolutely false"."In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town that took place, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything," he told the Sydney Morning Herald.Fast bowler Mitchell Starc has also denied having prior knowledge of the ball-tampering.In 2021, Starc and fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement. They said they did not know that a "foreign substance" had been taken onto the field to tamper with the ball during the Cape Town Test.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Mount Maunganui: The Indian team management is contemplating releasing Gurnoor Brar from the ODI squad.
articles.body: Mount Maunganui: The Indian team management is contemplating releasing Gurnoor Brar from the ODI squad. TimesofIndia.com has learnt that Brar could be released after the fourth ODI, with a final decision expected after Friday's fixture in Tauranga.With New Zealand having tall bowlers in their squad, the management is keen to have Brar with the Test squad in Wellington. The fast bowler is not part of the India Test squad but has been asked to stay back.India's batting coach Sitanshu Kotak confirmed that the support staff would split after the Hamilton ODI. Head coach Gautam Gambhir and spin bowling coach Sairaj Bahutule are with the ODI set-up, while Kotak, bowling coach Morne Morkel and fielding coach Subhadeep Ghosh are accompanying the Test squad.Gill, KL Rahul and Anshul Kamboj left Hamilton for Wellington, while the remaining players, who are part of the India A set-up, joined the group from Christchurch.Ruturaj Gaikwad likely to openAs far as the fourth ODI against New Zealand is concerned, India are likely to make two changes, with Ruturaj Gaikwad coming in as an opener in place of Shubman Gill, while Ishan Kishan is expected to retain his place in the middle order.A late shake-up cannot be ruled out, but cues from the nets and discussions within the group point to Kishan batting in the middle order for the remaining two ODIs.All the batters, including Tilak Varma, had extended batting sessions in the nets. Ruturaj looked assured and will be keen to make the most of the opportunities in the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Virat Kohli and the art of not ceding an inch
articles.summary: TimesofIndia.com in Mount Maunganui: Virat Kohli on Thursday meant business when the team assembled for training ahead of the fourth ODI against New
articles.body: TimesofIndia.com in Mount Maunganui: Virat Kohli on Thursday meant business when the team assembled for training ahead of the fourth ODI against New Zealand. From the moment he entered the covered nets area, the ODI stalwart was unusually chirpy as he faced the trio of Gurnoor Brar, Mohammed Siraj and Arshdeep Singh. Speaking fluent Punjabi, he questioned the fielding setup and gave feedback on bowling lengths to Brar and Arshdeep.Arshdeep, in particular, had an eventful contest with Kohli; the two were at it for close to twenty minutes. What started as friendly banter quickly turned into a fiery duel after the left-arm seamer cleaned up Kohli, leaving him in disbelief. Disgruntled, Kohli marched to the other end, making way for Rohit Sharma. Even while waiting for his turn, he kept thinking about the dismissal and punched his gloves together in frustration. The signal was clear: bring it on!One could sense the energy Kohli was riding after the blip, and he charged the first Arshdeep delivery he faced only to slice thin air. The bowler, too, kept playing along, finishing his follow-through next to the batter with his hands resting behind his head. The jibes continued in Punjabi but only lasted a few deliveries before Kohli moved to the net where the spinners Axar Patel, Naman Dhir and Kuldeep Yadav were operating. He was out of the firing line but kept needling Arshdeep after animated appeals."Hain? Howzat?" he would jokingly ask, even making a DRS gesture, when Arshdeep appealed during his spell. The youngster did have the last laugh, but Kohli wasn't done competing, and certainly not chatting.Round 2 happened with Kuldeep when the chinaman made the right-hander play one back to his stumps. As Kuldeep celebrated, Kohli played it down: “Ye koi ball thi wicket ki?," he said before deciding to pause.Arshdeep kept talking about length and mindset with Kohli, who shared his experience with the bowlers. He narrated an instance of facing a quick Jofra Archer delivery in the IPL that rose sharply from the good-length spot, stressing the importance of lengths, while assessing the pitch.It was a long hit for Kohli on Thursday. He faced a mix of fast bowling, spin and throwdowns, but he brought match-like energy, making it a very lively session for the squad. There was the occasional chatter with head coach Gautam Gambhir and plenty of laughs, but what stood out was his unwillingness to give an inch.No matter what he did or who he faced, Kohli simulated match-like energy in the semi-closed setting and didn't leave the facility without ticking off his required boxes. Right from the football session with Brar to his cool-down chat with stand-in skipper Shreyas Iyer, Kohli's afternoon had purpose written all over it. As he walked back, the fans wanted a piece of the Indian superstar.Patiently, he signed whatever came his way and called it a day.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Can't really target anyone individually': Tim Seifert explains why India's bowling attack has troubled New Zealand
articles.summary: New Zealand's batters have found little room to breathe against India's disciplined pace attack, and Tim Seifert believes the biggest challenge has been
articles.body: New Zealand's batters have found little room to breathe against India's disciplined pace attack, and Tim Seifert believes the biggest challenge has been the visitors' ability to operate as a unit rather than rely on one standout bowler.With India leading the five-match ODI series 2-0, the New Zealand wicketkeeper-batter admitted his side could not identify a particular Indian bowler to target, crediting the variety and consistency within the attack for putting the hosts under pressure.India's pace battery, featuring Arshdeep Singh, Anshul Kamboj, Auqib Nabi and Gurnoor Brar, has troubled New Zealand in the first two matches. Gurnoor has emerged as the leading wicket-taker in the series with seven scalps, while the third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned without a ball being bowled due to rain.'They work well as a unit': Seifert on India's pace attackSeifert pointed to the different qualities each Indian pacer brings to the attack, particularly highlighting the advantage of having a left-arm option in Arshdeep."They all bowl very well, they all do something slightly different. Having Arshdeep (Singh) as a left-hander, I think it's crucial as well. But to be honest, they work well as a unit. They all do something a little bit different," Seifert said during the pre-match press conference."To their credit, they didn't miss much on those wickets the last two games. I can't really target anyone individually; I think they do a very good job together," he added.New Zealand looking to regroup after 2-0 deficitDespite the results not going their way, Seifert said New Zealand had faced challenging batting conditions and were focused on making the most of the remaining two matches. The hosts have also undergone changes in personnel, with several players leaving the ODI squad to prepare for the upcoming Test series, which begins on November 19."It's good. I think, look, obviously the result hasn't necessarily gone our way, but we've obviously been put in some tricky situations with the wickets as well. So, look, it's a new bunch of guys here. A few guys have left for the Test series starting on November 19, so we're just focusing on the next two games ahead," he said.Seifert unfazed by changes in personnelAsked about the changes in personnel in both camps, Seifert said the challenge remained the same regardless of who featured in the playing XI. He insisted that every player coming into the side would be an international cricketer capable of making an impact, adding that New Zealand would approach the final two matches with the same competitive mindset."No matter who India play or whoever we play as well, we're out there for the challenge, and everyone's an international cricketer out there. So whoever steps into their role, they're going to try their best. Same with us, whoever steps into the role that the boys have left, everyone's going to try their best as well," he concluded.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: At 44, England great James Anderson extends playing career with Surrey after shock Lancashire departure
articles.summary: At 44, James Anderson is not ready to walk away from cricket.
articles.body: At 44, James Anderson is not ready to walk away from cricket. England's legendary fast bowler is set to begin a new chapter in his illustrious career after joining Surrey for the 2027 county season, following the end of his 25-year association with Lancashire.Surrey confirmed the signing on Thursday, giving the veteran pacer an opportunity to continue playing at the highest level of county cricket. Anderson's move comes after Lancashire decided against renewing his contract for the upcoming season, bringing an unexpected end to his long association with his boyhood club.Despite the disappointment, Anderson has made it clear that he still has the hunger to compete, take wickets and contribute to a team's success.'I still feel like I have a lot to offer': Anderson on Surrey moveAnderson expressed his excitement about joining Surrey and said he was looking forward to contributing both on and off the field."I still feel like I have a lot to offer, taking wickets, trying to help the team win games," Anderson said in a statement.The former England international also highlighted his desire to help younger players develop their skills and progress towards representing the national team."I also think that I can bring a lot to the team off the field and help those young players who are looking to develop their skillset and go on and represent their country," he added.According to British media reports, Anderson has signed an initial one-year deal with Surrey, with an option to extend his stay beyond the 2027 season.Lancashire exit ends 25-year associationAnderson's move to Surrey follows a difficult few weeks after Lancashire opted not to renew his contract. The decision ended a 25-year relationship with the county where he began his professional career in 2001. The veteran pacer admitted he was shocked by the decision but remained determined to explore new opportunities rather than bring his playing career to an end.His departure came despite an impressive 2026 County Championship campaign, during which he claimed 50 wickets. Anderson had also captained Lancashire during the season, making the decision not to retain him a significant development.The fast bowler will now bring his experience and leadership to Surrey as he looks to make an impact in the 2027 campaign.Anderson's remarkable international careerWidely regarded as one of the greatest fast bowlers in cricket history, Anderson retired from international cricket in 2024 after a career spanning more than two decades. He finished with 991 international wickets across formats, the highest tally by a fast bowler in men's international cricket. His Test record remains particularly remarkable, with 704 wickets in 188 matches, making him the most successful fast bowler in the history of the format.Anderson also claimed 269 ODI wickets and 18 T20I wickets for England. He made his international debut in 2002 and became the spearhead of England's pace attack across several generations.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Kusal Mendis scripts history, joins Virat Kohli, Steve Smith and Joe Root in elite club
articles.summary: Kusal Mendis joined an elite group featuring Joe Root, Virat Kohli and Steve Smith after becoming the latest batter to score a century on his debut as a
articles.body: Kusal Mendis joined an elite group featuring Joe Root, Virat Kohli and Steve Smith after becoming the latest batter to score a century on his debut as a Test captain. The Sri Lankan made history against Pakistan on Wednesday, becoming the first player from his country to achieve the feat.Mendis, who took over as Sri Lanka's full-time Test captain from Dhananjaya de Silva last month, marked his leadership debut with a memorable unbeaten hundred. His knock also placed him among the prominent names in world cricket who have begun their Test captaincy careers with a century.The 31-year-old reached the landmark with a boundary off Razaullah in the third delivery of the 92nd over.Mendis also played a crucial role in Sri Lanka's recovery after the visitors found themselves struggling at 155/4 in 42 overs. He combined with his fifth-wicket partner to put together a massive 249-run stand.With the achievement, Mendis became the 37th cricketer overall to register a hundred in his first Test as captain. He is also only the second player after former England skipper Andrew Strauss to score a century on his Test captaincy debut against Pakistan.The list of players to have accomplished the feat includes some of the biggest names in the game. India's Virat Kohli scored 115 against Australia in Adelaide in 2014, while Steve Smith followed with 133 against India in Brisbane later that month. England's Joe Root also made a memorable start to his captaincy tenure, scoring 190 against South Africa at Lord's in 2017.Other notable names on the list include Sunil Gavaskar, Greg Chappell, Alastair Cook, Kevin Pietersen and Shubman Gill, who scored 147 against England at Leeds in 2025. South Africa's Wiaan Mulder also made history with an unbeaten 367 against Zimbabwe in Bulawayo in 2025.Mendis' century also brought another significant personal milestone. During his innings, he crossed 13,000 runs in international cricket, becoming only the eighth Sri Lankan batter to reach the mark across all three formats.Kumar Sangakkara remains Sri Lanka's leading run-scorer in international cricket with 27,757 runs from 587 matches between 2000 and 2015. Mahela Jayawardene occupies second place with 25,688 runs, followed by Sanath Jayasuriya with 20,966.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Mate, well done': Australia captain Mitch Marsh responds to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims
articles.summary: Australia captain Mitch Marsh chose not to discuss the Sandpapergate scandal on Thursday, saying his focus was on leading the team in the upcoming
articles.body: Australia captain Mitch Marsh chose not to discuss the Sandpapergate scandal on Thursday, saying his focus was on leading the team in the upcoming white-ball series against England rather than revisiting events in Cape Town eight years ago.Marsh faced the media in Perth, five days after former Australia teammate Usman Khawaja brought the ball-tampering controversy back into the spotlight. In his autobiography, Khawaja claimed that the entire Australian squad knew about the plan to use sandpaper to rough up the ball during the 2018 Test against South Africa.The incident led to lengthy bans for three Australian players and had a major impact on cricket in the country. In the eight years since, Cricket Australia, the team management and several players have rarely spoken about the controversy. Members of Australia's bowling group have rejected claims that the entire team knew about the plan to use sandpaper to help the ball swing through the air.When asked about the scandal at the start of his scheduled press conference, Marsh responded: “You hit a six off the first ball there, Mate, well done!” He then added: “Look, obviously there's been a bit of noise around this week and I respect that certain people have told their stories."“I'm not here to share mine today, I know that might sound weird, but it's a big week for us and it's an important time for this one-day (squad) and my sole focus has been on preparing for tomorrow.”The controversy has dominated cricket coverage this week and is expected to remain a talking point as the Australian summer gets underway.Australia and England begin their white-ball series in Perth on Friday, with three ODIs and five T20Is scheduled between the teams. Meanwhile, Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is set to address the controversy at a press conference in Sydney, hours before the opening match.Cummins said he had taken time to understand Khawaja's claims before responding. “Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week,” Cummins posted on X. “I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly.”What happened in the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal?Steve Smith and David Warner, who were Australia's captain and vice-captain at the time, were each handed 12-month bans by Cricket Australia following an investigation into the ball-tampering incident. Cameron Bancroft, who was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match, received a nine-month ban.Smith and Warner returned to the Australian team in 2019. Smith continues to play Test cricket for the country and is preparing for a four-match series against New Zealand starting next month.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Pakistan's Saqib Khan wreaks havoc against Sri Lanka on Day 4, enters record books with seven-wicket haul
articles.summary: Pakistan fast bowler Saqib Khan made an immediate impact on his Test debut, claiming a sensational seven-wicket haul to turn the first Test against Sri
articles.body: Pakistan fast bowler Saqib Khan made an immediate impact on his Test debut, claiming a sensational seven-wicket haul to turn the first Test against Sri Lanka in the hosts' favour on a rain-interrupted fourth day at Rawalpindi on Thursday.The 31-year-old pacer returned impressive figures of 7/130 as Sri Lanka, who had resumed the day at a commanding 404/4, were bowled out for 446. The visitors managed to secure only a slender 12-run first-innings advantage after losing their final six wickets for just 42 runs.Pakistan responded with 57/1 in 21.2 overs in their second innings before bad light and subsequent rain brought an early end to proceedings at 3:05 pm. The hosts now hold a 45-run lead, with Azan Awais and Mohammad Taha at the crease.Awais was batting on 22 after being given a reprieve when Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis dropped him behind the stumps on 17. Taha, one of four Pakistan players making their Test debuts in the match, remained unbeaten on 24 off 55 deliveries, having already registered a half-century in the first innings.Saqib's performance made him only the fourth Pakistani bowler to take seven wickets in an innings on Test debut. He joined Mohammad Nazir, Mohammad Zahid and Abrar Ahmed in the exclusive list.The right-arm pacer attributed his success to exploiting the conditions and sticking to his natural strengths, particularly his ability to generate outswing.“My strength is to bowl out-swingers and I did exactly that today under favorable overcast conditions,” Saqib said.“Yesterday was a bad day for us because we couldn't bowl the way we would have liked to, but coach Mike Hesson told us in the dressing room that if we hit the off stump line and bowl out-swingers we will get wickets.”Saqib dismantles Sri Lanka's batting lineupAfter struggling to make breakthroughs on the previous day, Pakistan's bowlers found the assistance they needed from the surface on Thursday. The overcast conditions brought the greenish pitch to life, allowing Saqib to trouble the Sri Lankan batters with movement off the surface.He produced a devastating eight-over spell, picking up five wickets for just 25 runs. The breakthrough came almost immediately as he ended Dhananjaya de Silva's marathon innings of 167, breaking the 249-run fifth-wicket partnership with Mendis.Sri Lanka's captain followed soon after. Saud Shakeel missed another opportunity when he put down a low catch off Mendis, but wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori made no mistake two deliveries later, completing an impressive diving catch off Saqib. Mendis departed for 119.The debutant continued his remarkable spell by removing Sonal Dinusha, who had been in impressive form with three centuries and two half-centuries in his previous five Tests. The left-hander made 20 before edging an expansive drive into the slips. Saqib celebrated his fifth wicket by kissing the pitch.Milan Rathnayake briefly kept Sri Lanka moving towards a bigger total, taking the visitors past Pakistan's first-innings score of 434/9 declared with a boundary off Razaullah. However, Saqib returned to claim two more wickets, including that of Asitha Fernando, who was caught behind by Ghori.Razaullah then brought Sri Lanka's innings to a close by dismissing Rathnayake, who top-edged a pull shot towards deep fine leg.Pakistan hold the advantage despite early setbackPakistan also lost a wicket during their second innings, with debutant Tayyab Arif trapped in front by Fernando for 11 in the third over. Arif's dismissal came after Pakistan had used one of their three available reviews unsuccessfully.However, Awais and Taha showed patience in challenging batting conditions, preventing Sri Lanka from making further inroads before the weather intervened.With a 45-run advantage and nine wickets remaining, Pakistan will look to build on Saqib's outstanding contribution when play resumes on the final day.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: India Under-19 secured their place in the ACC Men's U19 Asia Cup 2026 final with a convincing eight-wicket victory over Afghanistan in the semifinal at Al Amerat, Oman, on Thursday.Chasing a target of 228, India reached 230/2 in just 36.5 overs, with captain Lakshya Raichandani leading the way with a match-winning unbeaten 93. The emphatic victory helped India seal their place in the final with 79 balls to spare.Afghanistan lose momentum after promising startAfghanistan, after winning the toss and electing to bat, made a steady start and appeared well placed to post a challenging total. At 143/3 in the 36th over, they had enough wickets in hand to accelerate during the final overs.However, India's bowlers turned the game around with a disciplined spell in the middle and death overs. Afghanistan lost three wickets in quick succession, with Aryan Savsani striking twice in the same over to dismiss Amir Hamza and Tahir Sarwary.Noman Salarzai and Shah Faisal Rahimi both scored 51, but struggled to accelerate against India's disciplined bowling attack. Captain Sohail Khan remained unbeaten on 36 off 44 deliveries, helping Afghanistan reach 227/8 in their allotted 50 overs.Ishan Sood was India's leading wicket-taker with figures of 3/43, while Savsani claimed 2/29. Manal Chauhan and Yashbardhan Chauhan also played their part in keeping Afghanistan's scoring rate under control.Raichandani, Sehwag and Vineeth power India's chaseIndia's response was built around an impressive opening partnership between Raichandani and Sehwag. The Indian skipper took an attacking approach from the outset, finding boundaries regularly, particularly through the off-side, while Sehwag provided stability at the other end.The pair added 117 runs for the opening wicket before Sehwag departed shortly after bringing up his half-century. His 51 off 57 balls provided the perfect platform for India's chase.Raichandani continued to dominate the Afghanistan bowlers and was joined by Vineeth, who rotated the strike effectively while capitalising on scoring opportunities. The Indian captain eventually fell for 93 off 90 deliveries, missing out on a well-deserved century by just seven runs.Vineeth ensured there were no further setbacks, bringing up his half-century before finishing the contest in style with a six off Noor Ali Niazi. He remained unbeaten on 57 as India completed a comprehensive victory in 36.5 overs.India set up final clash against PakistanThe victory sets up a high-profile India-Pakistan final on Saturday, giving the defending runners-up an opportunity to avenge their defeat in the previous edition's title clash, where Pakistan emerged champions.Brief Scores:Afghanistan U19: 227/8 in 50 overs (Noman Salarzai 51, Shah Faisal Rahimi 51; Ishan Sood 3/43, Aryan Savsani 2/29)India U19: 230/2 in 36.5 overs (Lakshya Raichandani 93, VK Vineeth 57*; Sohail Khan 1/56, Noor Ali Niazi 1/58)Result: India U19 won by eight wickets.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Simon Taufel returns to lead ILT20 match officials' panel for Season 5
articles.summary: One of cricket's most respected match officials, Australia’s Simon Taufel, will return to lead the match officials’ panel at the ILT20 for a fifth
articles.body: One of cricket's most respected match officials, Australia’s Simon Taufel, will return to lead the match officials’ panel at the ILT20 for a fifth consecutive season.The five-time ICC Umpire of the Year (2004–2008) will be the match referee for the season opener on 21 November at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium, where defending champions Desert Vipers take on MI Emirates in a rematch of last season’s final. Taufel will share match referee duties through the season with Roshan Mahanama (52 Tests and 213 ODIs for Sri Lanka).New Zealand’s Chris Brown, and Martin Saggers (three Tests for England) will be the on-field umpires for the opener. Australia’s Paul Wilson will be the third umpire and New Zealand’s Wayne Knights the fourth umpire.Wilson will alternate as third umpire (TV umpire) with West Indies’ Leslie Reifer for the competition. Both have been appointed as specialist TV umpires, with the ILT20 leveraging the HE Smart Replay system to enhance the accuracy and time efficiency of third-umpire decision-making.The panel also includes ICC Elite Panel umpires Richard Illingworth (nine Tests and 25 ODIs for England) and South Africa’s Adrian Holdstock, along with Afghanistan’s Ahmad Pakteen. Aasif Iqbal, Akbar Ali Khan and Shiju Mannil represent the UAE.To help develop officiating in the region, and as part of their wider partnership, the ILT20 will invite two umpires each from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia to shadow the panel during the league stage. They will attend matches to gain first-hand exposure to officiating at a higher level. The programme will be supported by former ICC Umpires Coach Dennis Burns.Ahead of the season, Taufel said: “It’s a privilege to return for a fifth season of the ILT20. We’re strengthened this year by ICC Elite Panel umpires Richard Illingworth and Adrian Holdstock, alongside Roshan Mahanama, talented umpires from across the world, and an ever-improving group of UAE officials. Our focus remains to keep the spotlight on the players and the quality of cricket through officiating excellence.”On the programme for Kuwaiti and Saudi umpires, Taufel added: “Bringing umpires from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia into our environment is a really exciting step for officiating in the region. Working alongside an international panel and learning from someone like Dennis Burns will give them exposure they can take back home and build on.”The updated Season 5 Playing Conditions also take effect from the opening match. The biggest on-field change is a new “batter zone” for judging wides on both sides, and umpires have been told to apply it strictly to stop negative bowling. The 60-second stop clock between overs now applies to the batting side as well. After two warnings in an innings, the fielding side will be awarded five penalty runs.ILT20 Season 5 will feature some of the game’s biggest stars, including Moeen Ali, Usman Tariq and Finn Allen (Abu Dhabi Knight Riders), Babar Azam, Shimron Hetmyer and Naseem Shah (Desert Vipers), Faf du Plessis, Marcus Stoinis and Mustafizur Rahman (Dubai Capitals), Heinrich Klaasen, Liam Livingstone and David Miller (Gulf Giants), Rashid Khan, Nicholas Pooran and Fazalhaq Farooqi (MI Emirates), and Mohammad Nabi, Sikandar Raza and Adil Rashid (Sharjah Warriorz).Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Sandpaper-gate takes another turn as former coach accused of asking Steve Smith, Cameron Bancroft not to reveal truth
articles.summary: The 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal has resurfaced with fresh allegations, eight years after the infamous Sandpaper-gate incident rocked
articles.body: The 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal has resurfaced with fresh allegations, eight years after the infamous Sandpaper-gate incident rocked international cricket. Former Australia bowling coach David Saker has reportedly been accused of urging Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft not to disclose that sandpaper was used to tamper with the ball during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.The latest development follows revelations in former Australian batter Usman Khawaja's memoir, Sabr, in which he claimed that the ball-tampering operation was not limited to a handful of players and that the entire Australian team was aware of the practice. Khawaja also questioned why Bancroft, Smith and David Warner were the only players to face sanctions for an incident that, according to him, involved a wider group within the dressing room.A report by the Sydney Morning Herald has now identified Saker as the unnamed coach repeatedly referenced in Khawaja's book, adding another dimension to the controversy.Saker allegedly told Smith and Bancroft not to mention sandpaperAccording to the report, Saker urged Smith and Bancroft not to reveal the identity of the yellow object taken onto the field at Newlands during their media interaction on the day the scandal came to light. The report further alleged that Saker repeatedly told the two players, "you can't say sandpaper" ahead of the infamous press conference.It was only after Cricket Australia announced disciplinary action against Smith, Bancroft and Warner that the use of sandpaper was publicly acknowledged. The report also claimed that Smith and Bancroft were advised by others not to lie during the press conference. However, Bancroft maintained that the object was tape when questioned by the media.Khawaja's memoir makes fresh revelations about dressing-room involvementAlthough Khawaja did not identify Saker by name in Sabr, he referred to an unnamed coach while recounting the events leading up to the ball-tampering incident. In one passage, Khawaja described a conversation between Bancroft and a coach during the lunch break before the latter was caught using sandpaper."With a smile on his face, he said, ‘Bangers, whatever you’re doing, we need more of it. It’s wet out there – we just need more of it'. Then I saw Bangers pick up a piece of sandpaper and put it in his pocket. The coach gave both me and Cameron a wry smile of satisfaction and walked away," Khawaja wrote.The former Australia opener also recalled the coach encouraging the bowling group to find ways to generate reverse swing, even if it meant taking unconventional measures."Guys, I don’t care what happens, but Test cricketers are too good against the straight ball," the coach was quoted as saying in the memoir."We need to get the ball shifting when it gets old. I don’t care what you have to do, or how, but we need to get it moving in the air. That’s the only chance we have," the unnamed coach reportedly added.Saker, who played a key role in England's historic Ashes triumph in Australia in 2010-11 as bowling coach, also worked with the England team during the 2013, 2023 and 2025-26 Ashes campaigns.He reportedly signed a non-disclosure agreement with Cricket Australia after leaving the organisation in February 2019.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Australia have begun shaping their batting plans for the 2027 ODI World Cup, with stand-in captain Mitchell Marsh identifying the top six he expects to form the core of the team's campaign. With limited opportunities to experiment in the format before the global tournament, Marsh indicated that the combination set to feature against England is likely to remain Australia's preferred batting line-up.According to Cricinfo, the first ODI against England in Perth on Friday will offer a glimpse of Australia's potential World Cup combination, with Marsh, Travis Head, Cooper Connolly, Matt Renshaw, Josh Inglis and Cameron Green expected to occupy the top six positions.With Australia not scheduled to play another ODI series until mid-2027, the upcoming three-match series against England will be an important opportunity for the team to build combinations ahead of the World Cup.Marsh backs Australia's preferred batting combinationMarsh expressed confidence in the current batting group, suggesting that the players selected for the England series are likely to form the backbone of Australia's World Cup plans."We've got a batting line-up that I see being at that World Cup, and it's sort of where we end up," Marsh said ahead of the ODI series, as quoted by Cricinfo.The absence of Steven Smith, who no longer plays ODI cricket, and Marnus Labuschagne, who has not featured in the format since July, has also brought the current batting combination into sharper focus. Labuschagne was part of Australia's 2023 ODI World Cup-winning squad but has endured a difficult run of form in recent months, which also saw him lose his place in the Test team.Australia rest senior fast bowlers ahead of England seriesWhile Australia are looking to settle their batting combination, their bowling attack will be without some of its biggest names for the series. articles.title: ‘I wasn't in that dressing room’: Harry Brook distances himself from Australia's ball-tampering scandal
articles.summary: England captain Harry Brook has chosen to stay out of the fresh controversy surrounding Australia's 2018 ball-tampering scandal, stating that he has never
articles.body: England captain Harry Brook has chosen to stay out of the fresh controversy surrounding Australia's 2018 ball-tampering scandal, stating that he has never witnessed any form of ball tampering during his international career. With Usman Khawaja's autobiography bringing the infamous Sandpapergate episode back into the spotlight, Brook made it clear that he had no direct knowledge of what happened in the Australian dressing room.The England skipper was speaking ahead of the first ODI against Australia at Perth Stadium on Friday when he was asked about the renewed debate surrounding the Cape Town Test against South Africa in March 2018. Brook pointed out that he was only around 17 or 18 at the time and was not involved in the events that shook Australian cricket."I've never seen any ball tampering before. I wasn't in that (Australia) dressing room. I think I was about 17 or 18 years old, so I was completely oblivious to any of that stuff," Brook said during the pre-match press conference, as quoted by The Independent.Rather than commenting further on the allegations and revelations from eight years ago, Brook preferred to shift the focus towards England's upcoming white-ball challenge. He stressed that his team needed to concentrate on its preparations for a demanding series against Australia on their home turf."We're here in Australia, we're looking forward to this series, and all we can do is concentrate on ourselves and getting ourselves as ready as possible. We're just trying to concentrate on ourselves at the minute. That's all we can do. We're here to play against a strong Australian side in their backyard," he added.Khawaja's autobiography reignites Sandpapergate debateThe controversy returned to the headlines following the publication of excerpts from Khawaja's recently released autobiography. The former Australia opener claimed that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.Khawaja also alleged that the ball-tampering tactic had been employed during the preceding Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, adding another dimension to the long-running controversy.Former Australia opener David Warner subsequently supported Khawaja's revelations. Warner was among the players punished following the scandal, receiving a one-year ban from international cricket and a lifetime leadership ban. The latter restriction was overturned in 2024.Brook excited about Perth challengeAway from the controversy, Brook expressed enthusiasm about leading England into the opening ODI, particularly at a venue that holds positive memories for him from the previous Ashes contest.The England captain described the Australia-England rivalry as a special one and said his team was eager to get the series underway at Optus Stadium."Australia against England is always a good series, and we're looking forward to kickstarting it. We're very happy to be out here. We're all really raring to go here at Optus Stadium, which is where the last Ashes started. It's an amazing place to play cricket. The atmosphere when we played here was unbelievable," he said.With the opening encounter set to take place in Perth, Brook's immediate attention remains on the cricket, despite the renewed scrutiny surrounding one of the most controversial episodes in Australia's cricketing history.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) chairman Mohsin Naqvi has indicated that the investigation into players Mohammad Rizwan and Imam-ul-Haq over alleged dressing-room leaks is nearing completion, with the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) expected to submit its findings within the next few days.The two Pakistan cricketers came under investigation following the team's 0-3 Test series defeat against England. articles.body: South Africa are likely to receive a major boost to their pace attack for the second Test against Bangladesh, with Anrich Nortje on course to return from a groin injury. Head coach Shukri Conrad confirmed that the fast bowler is recovering well and could be available for the series' second match at SuperSport Park in Centurion.Nortje picked up the injury during the second Test against Australia in Gqeberha but scans revealed that the damage was less serious than initially feared. The 32-year-old will miss the series opener at the Wanderers, which begins on Sunday, November 15, but is expected to be fit for the second Test starting November 23."He went for the scan at St George’s during the Test match, and it revealed nothing sinister. It wasn’t as bad as initially anticipated and didn’t require anything out of the ordinary either, just a little bit of rest and then some rehab," Conrad was quoted as saying by cricinfo on Thursday."He’ll definitely be in the frame for one of the Test matches here, possibly the second one. From a medical point of view, there was nothing wrong, and he’s recovered well. He’s started training early enough. He’s building up his loads as we speak and he should be good to go by the second Test," he added.Corbin Bosch, Dane Paterson in contention for opening TestWith Nortje unavailable for the first Test, Corbin Bosch and Dane Paterson are the leading contenders for the third seamer's position alongside South Africa's established pace options. However, Conrad ruled out the possibility of fielding an all-pace attack, insisting that the team would not necessarily benefit from playing five specialist fast bowlers.The South African coach highlighted Wiaan Mulder's ability to contribute with the ball, which provides the team with the flexibility to include a specialist spinner in the playing XI."What’s a full pace attack? Is it four or five? Even if you go with five quicks, someone’s not going to bowl his overs," Conrad said."What Wiaan does, in particular with the ball now, is that he gives you the luxury of playing a specialist spinner. A fifth seamer, for me, is a bit of a waste because if the four aren’t going to bowl a side out, trust me, the fifth one’s not going to do that. There’ll be no temptation to play five seamers," he added.Shukri Conrad expects balanced Wanderers pitchThe Wanderers has offered some assistance to spinners in recent years, but thunderstorms are forecast throughout the five-day Test, potentially bringing the fast bowlers into play. Conrad, however, is hoping for a balanced surface with good pace and bounce, allowing both batters and bowlers to make an impact."It's stock standard. It’s obviously hot here. We just hope that it’s not over-prepared and ready too early. It’s got a really good grass covering," he said."I’d like to think we’ll get a Wanderers wicket of old where there’s good pace and balance because I think our attack can bowl on good wickets. We can take 20 wickets on good wickets. And we certainly want to give our batters every chance of posting big totals," Conrad added.South Africa vs Bangladesh: Test series scheduleThe two-match Test series will begin at the Wanderers in Johannesburg on November 15, with the second and final Test scheduled to take place at SuperSport Park in Centurion from November 23.MatchDateVenue1st TestNovember 15-19Wanderers, Johannesburg2nd TestNovember 23-27SuperSport Park, CenturionGet the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Pat Cummins calls Usman Khawaja sandpaper claims 'wrong' and 'nonsense'
articles.summary: Australia captain Pat Cummins hits back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja’s claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them “100% wrong” and “utter nonsense”.
articles.body:
Australia captain Pat Cummins has hit back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".

In 2018, Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished for a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Khawaja has published his autobiography this week and the former batter has said the entire Australia team, which included Cummins, knew about the sandpaper scheme and should have taken responsibility.

But in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney, Cummins countered and said: "When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong.

"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins and Khawaja played 56 Tests together until Khawaja retired from international cricket in January.

Khawaja was in the Australia XI when Cummins made his Test debut in 2011 and the pair were also once team-mates in domestic cricket with New South Wales.

"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," said Cummins.

"In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others - and, I think, Australian cricket.

"I support him to tell his story, 100%, I'm glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

In a media conference he arranged himself, Cummins began by promising to answer all questions because, he said: "I don't want to talk about this again after today."

At times emotional, Cummins addressed a wide range of topics, including:

Advice that some of Khawaja's claims are defamatory, but he will not take legal action

He had been in contact with Khawaja and Smith since the book was published, but not Warner

His belief that the one-year bans handed to Smith and Warner, and a nine-month suspension to Bancroft were "heavy handed"

He had no recollection of Australia tampering with the ball in the 2017-18 Ashes series against England

He had met with Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg, who has reviewed the files from the original investigation

Explaining why sandpaper would have been present in the dressing room and that it was sometimes used by bowlers in training in order to practise with a reverse-swinging ball

Khawaja's allegations have reopened the debate about the sandpaper plot, the investigation into the cheating, the culture of Australian cricket and the reputations of those involved.

The story has dominated the media in Australia and caused headlines around the cricketing world.

Khawaja has been supported by Warner and Chadd Sayers, a seam bowler who was part of the Australia squad on the 2018 tour of South Africa.

However, his allegations have been rejected by Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach and former England batter Graeme Hick, one of Lehmann's assistants. Mitchell Starc, another bowler on the tour, has also denied Khawaja's claims.

Khawaja has put a spotlight on Cummins and his fellow bowlers Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon. The four were Australia's attack in Cape Town and remain their first-choice bowlers eight years later.

The quartet have always denied any knowledge of the plot, including in the release of a joint-statement in 2021.

In his book - Sabr - Khawaja alleged Australia were urged to find ways of getting the ball to swing by a coach, while Bancroft was later encouraged to cheat.

Khawaja also said he asked for the entire team to take responsibility for the controversy in Cape Town, but his request was rejected by two unnamed players.

Cummins said he does not recall any suggestion that the team should have shared the responsibility, or that it was rejected.

On the idea that the whole team were aligned in a plot to tamper with the ball, he said: "There was no masterplan around using illegal methods. People assume you've gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge masterplan.

"That is not the case. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen."

"There's big leaps where Usman is being vague."

In his book, Khawaja detailed how he was not interviewed as part of the investigation despite sitting next to Bancroft in the changing rooms during the Test at Newlands.

Both Khawaja and Warner have criticised the investigation, which Greenberg has said he will not reopen.

Cummins confirmed he has met with Greenberg and, although the captain said he did not want to break a "confidence", that Greenberg has reviewed the sandpaper files since the release of Khawaja's book and found the accounts in the investigation to be "consistent".

Cummins has played 77 Tests for Australia and has been captain sine 2021. He said he has seen only one instance of ball-tampering in his career, during a domestic Sheffield Shield match, when a player took a bottletop on to the field.

However, he did admit that balls can sometimes be altered during training sessions, if bowlers want to practise in a certain way, or batters want to face a ball of a particular condition.

Cummins said it was not unknown for training balls to be scuffed in such circumstances, using sandpaper or even a Stanley knife.

When it was put to Cummins that he, as a bowler, must have suspected that the Cape Town ball had been tampered with, the 33-year-old described that bowlers often touch a ball as little as possible, in order to keep it dry and in a state where it will reverse-swing.

At the time of the sandpaper scandal, Cummins was 24 and playing in his 13th Test. Asked about a potential culture of ball-tampering in that era, Cummins said he noticed things then that he now realises could have been cheating.

On why Khawaja has chosen to speak now, at the end of his career, rather than in the intervening eight years, Cummins said the episode could have "weighed heavy" on the left-hander.

Addressing the culture of the Australia team eight years ago, Cummins said: "I didn't like the way we spoke to umpires, the opposition. I think there was a bit of an arrogance and a bit of an ugliness at times that didn't sit well with me as a young guy.

"Now I'm captain, I have spent a lot of time making sure that that's not the case."

Analysis - Cummins did not dodge a single question

Khawaja's claims - in his book, in interviews and on social media - have re-opened old wounds in Australian cricket, drawing battlelines that have verged on civil war.

Over the past few days, constant questions have been asked of who knew what and if the truth has been covered up in the intervening eight years.

The most pressure has been on the bowlers who played for Australia in Cape Town, - none more so than Cummins, given his rise to the captaincy.

He has been urged to front up, to show leadership. In a remarkable news conference in an indoor cricket centre in Sydney, Cummins did just that.

Others connected to the scandal who have faced the media in the past few days – Lehmann, Starc and Mitchell Marsh – have almost implicated themselves with vague responses to straight questions. Not Cummins.

The captain did not duck or dodge any of the subjects that were thrown at him by a huge throng of assembled journalists. He did so without any intervention from a media manager.

What was most striking was his criticism of Khawaja, once a team-mate and friend. In being so forceful of his rejection of what Khawaja has claimed, Cummins appeared to be a reliable witness.

The question is whether this will be enough to end the speculation. Khawaja is sure to have another say. So too Warner, who is yet to release a book of his own.

Cummins cannot prove a negative, so can use only his words when it comes to convincing the world he was not involved in the sandpaper plot.

On this occasion, Cummins was impressive. Still, when he says he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, that feels like wishful thinking.

articles.title: Sandpapergate: Australia Test captain Pat Cummins dismisses Usman Khawaja's claims over ball-tampering scandal as 'utter nonsense'
articles.summary: Usman Khawaja said in new book 'Sabr' that every Australia player was aware of ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018; current Test captain Pat Cummins, who played in the match, reiterated his denial of involvement and dismissed Khawaja's claims as "utter nonsense"
articles.body:
Khawaja made the revelations in his new book 'Sabr', which was released earlier this week, bringing the scandal back onto the agenda eight years after Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera using sandpaper on the ball while Australia were fielding.

Only Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and his vice-captain David Warner were punished, with each receiving lengthy bans as the rest of the Australian team and coaching staff denied knowledge of the scheme.

Cummins, who was a relatively junior member of the side playing in just his 13th Test match, in 2021 issued a joint-statement with fellow bowlers from the fixture Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the ball in order to try to make it swing.

"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, ​he's 100 per cent wrong. I've said that consistently for the last eight years," ‌Cummins told reporters on Friday morning in Sydney having called the press conference himself on social media.

"I did not know that was happening, but Usman actually says things that ​are actually far more serious than that.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

Following the publication of the book, Warner, who received a year-long ban from all cricket and a lifetime ban from leadership roles, said on Monday that Khawaja's version of events was "100 per cent accurate" .

Cummins, who was appointed Australia captain in November 2021, criticised Khawaja for being "casual" with the lives of his former team-mates and Australian cricket as a whole.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and ​reputations," Cummins said.

"In his book, Ussie has been casual with my life and the ​lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket."

Cummins, who appeared to become emotional at times in a press conference that lasted more than an hour, revealed that a video taken of him and his wife Becky in a heated discussion a day earlier had been prompted by her anger with Khawaja's actions.

Despite that and his clear disagreement with Khawaja's statements, Cummins said that he does not intend to pursue legal action.

"I did get advised this week that some of the things ​that've been said are probably defamatory, but I won't be doing that," Cummins said.

"You've got to move on. It's been eight years. We're moving on. So ‌you got to draw a line ​at some point."

Cummins has been rested for England's white-ball tour of Australia, which resulted in him holding his press conference on Friday morning in Sydney just hours before the first ODI was scheduled to begin in Perth.

How have other Australian players reacted?

Cummins' extraordinary press conference came a day after Australia ODI captain Mitchell Marsh, who was also part of the team that toured South Africa in 2018, declined to comment on a series of questions about Khawaja's book.

Khawaja also claimed in the book that Australia experimented with lifting the seam on the ball during the 2017-18 Ashes at home to England, which they won 4-0 under the captaincy of Smith.

Starc, who had spoken to reporters on Tuesday, took a similar line to Cummins as he insisted that his recollections hadn't changed.

Starc, who is also not part of Australia's limited-overs side to face England, said of Khawaja's claims: "I haven't really paid much attention to it to be fair.

"There are differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process, at the time and since.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but from where I stand my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field. That's where I'll leave it.

"I will be sticking to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time eight years ago, so clearly there are differing versions from different people.

"We weren't aware of anything taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town.

"As far as the book is concerned, I haven't read it. I probably won't read it, so that's for Usman to elaborate on."

articles.title: What Pat Cummins said about Usman Khawaja and sandpaper scandal: Key points from explosive presser
articles.summary: Australia captain Pat Cummins has strongly rejected Usman Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian team knew about the use of sandpaper during the 2018
articles.body: Australia captain Pat Cummins has strongly rejected Usman Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian team knew about the use of sandpaper during the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa.Cummins addressed the allegations during a 68-minute press conference at Cricket Central in Sydney. He called Khawaja's claims "100% wrong" and "complete and utter nonsense".Khawaja, in his recently published autobiography, alleged that the entire Australia XI knew about the use of sandpaper in the Cape Town Test. He also claimed that two players had refused to take collective responsibility for the incident.Cummins responded to several allegations, spoke about the 2018 investigation, his relationship with Khawaja, the punishments handed to Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft, and his current relationship with Smith.Key points from Pat Cummins' press conferenceDid the entire Australian team know about the sandpaper?Cummins strongly denied Khawaja's claim that all 11 players knew sandpaper was being used to tamper with the ball during the Cape Town Test in 2018."When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong," Cummins said. "I've said that consistently for the last eight years, I did not know that was happening."But I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that."He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense. I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper."That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that I think, or that has been part of a team that's helped rebuild this Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and you know the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then. Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations."In his book, Ussie has been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket."I support his right to tell a story 100%. I'm really glad that he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do." Was there a master-plan to tamper with the ball?Cummins admitted that the Australian team had a win-at-all-costs mentality in 2018. He also spoke about an "ugly underbelly" and too many groups within the team. However, he rejected the suggestion that there was a planned effort to use illegal methods to make the ball reverse."There was no master-plan around using illegal methods," Cummins said. "I think that's maybe something that hasn't been spoken about enough. People assume you've gone from very legal methods [to get the ball to reverse] to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge master-plan."The truth, that is not the case."That's one of the reasons why I really want to talk through [it], because context and details matter around this. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen. I think there's natural progressions that get you there."Did Cummins know about sandpaper being used before the Port Elizabeth Test?Khawaja also alleged that sandpaper had been used on the ball near the boundary before the start of a session during the Port Elizabeth Test, now known as Gqeberha. That match took place before the Cape Town Test.Cummins said this was new information for him and that he was surprised by the claim."That was news to me this week," Cummins said. "I had no idea. Even chatting a couple of guys, that was a revelation to us. That was one of the things that really surprised me because that doesn't happen anymore."The umpires give the ball out to you in the middle, so I don't remember that. I remember growing up, used to watch for the umpire dropping the ball, but I genuinely don't remember that being the case. I don't know where that stopped. So that was a revelation to me this week."Had Cummins ever seen ball-tampering during his career?Cummins said the only time he had seen someone use an illegal object to change the condition of the ball was early in his career in a Sheffield Shield match.He recalled a senior New South Wales batter using a bottle cap on the ball. However, he refused to reveal the player's name or the match."He was a batter," Cummins said. "He was a senior player, I won't mention him, but he took a bottle cap out in the field, and that was the one time I've seen on the field. I was looking at it going, 'Wow, that's not okay.' It was dealt with. The umpires knew it as well. They called him out and said, 'You've got to stop that right now.' He was dealt with. That's the only time I've seen something illegal out there."Did two players refuse to take collective responsibility?Khawaja claimed that he had asked the Australian team to take collective responsibility for the ball-tampering incident in Cape Town. He also alleged that two players had refused to support his suggestion.Cummins said he did not remember any such discussion or team meeting."First part, I don't remember any conversation around collective responsibility," Cummins said. "I don't remember any team meeting where he stood up and said, 'Let's all own this as a team'. So then, to follow on, no, I've got no idea who those two people would be because I don't remember ever being asked or having a conversation about it."I've spoken to quite a few other people, and [they are] exactly the same. Trying to piece it all together, no one remembers a team meeting where someone stood up and said, 'We got to all own this.'"Was Cummins interviewed during the original investigation?Cummins confirmed that he was interviewed as part of Cricket Australia's investigation into the Cape Town incident.The investigation was conducted by Cricket Australia's then-head of integrity Iain Roy and High Performance manager Pat Howard.Cummins said the bowlers were among those specifically asked to take part. He added that other players were also given an opportunity to share information."I got asked to be part of that review," Cummins said. "There were some people that got specifically asked. I think it was the bowlers, and I can't really remember who else. And then I remember specifically a couple of times [them] saying, 'If anyone else has different accounts, or anyone else has information they'd like to share, please come forward and do that.' I did my interview. I was totally truthful. I've been very consistent since then at that event till now. Nothing's changed."Why was Khawaja not interviewed in the investigation?Khawaja alleged in his book that he was not interviewed during the original investigation, despite sitting next to Bancroft in the Cape Town dressing room.Cummins said he had spoken to Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg before the press conference to confirm his recollection of the investigation."I actually even spoke to Todd today," Cummins said. "He's like, 'I've read all the investigations. Guys have been very, very consistent this whole time.'"Should Cricket Australia reopen the investigation?Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg had said earlier in the week that the governing body would not reopen the investigation.When asked whether the investigation should be conducted again, Cummins said the decision was up to Cricket Australia."That's up to CA," Cummins said. "Part of why I think this is still lingering after eight years is there's a lot of context around this, which is hard to explain and hard to articulate, and that's what I want to do today. But there's a very proper way to do things and an improper [way], and I think that investigation was the proper way to do it. Everyone was asked in the circumstances, with a game very quickly after, so yeah, that's for CA. I think you could maybe argue whether the judgments were fair, but what can you do? I got asked all the questions, and answered them all fairly."Has Cummins spoken to Khawaja? Will he take legal action?Cummins confirmed that he had spoken to Khawaja during the week but did not reveal what they discussed.He admitted that he was still trying to understand how the allegations would affect their long-standing friendship.Cummins also said he had been advised that some of Khawaja's claims were "probably defamatory". However, he ruled out taking legal action."You've got to move on," he said. "It's been eight years … You got to draw the line at some point. I won't be doing that."Why does Cummins feel Khawaja's claims are irresponsible?Cummins spoke about his long friendship with Khawaja, who has been part of his cricket journey for 15 years.However, he said the allegations were serious because they affected the lives and reputations of several people and their families."I've played 15 years, my debut for New South Wales and with Australia, Usman was right there, and he's been awesome to me, and he's a friend," Cummins said. "But this is people's real lives, and this is serious. I saw [my wife] Becky on the news yesterday. Like this affects not only people but people's families, and I'm one of the lesser ones. Maybe this week I'm right there. But talking eight years ago, like it was traumatic for those guys, for all of us, for Australian cricket, for fans. So to bring it up so flippantly and casually, I think it's irresponsible. So yeah, they're all things I'm grappling with at the moment."Were the punishments handed to Smith, Warner and Bancroft too harsh?Cummins made his position clear on the punishments given to Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft following the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.He believed the bans handed to the three players were too severe.Cummins also said he had not spoken to Warner or Bancroft since Khawaja's book was released. However, he said he had no issues with Bancroft, despite the batter's 2021 interview with The Guardian, in which he claimed it was "self-explanatory" that the bowling group knew about the sandpaper.Cummins said the punishments were "way too heavy-handed" and "way over the top."What is Cummins' relationship with Steve Smith now?Cummins confirmed that he had spoken to Smith several times since the recent controversy.Smith had withdrawn from the third Test in South Africa due to a neck injury. There had also been suggestions of frustration within the Australian camp following his withdrawal.Cummins said their relationship was in a good place and that they were on the same page."I've spoken to Steve a few times since," Cummins said. "He's good. He's saying his neck is feeling better. I think he gets into Australia very soon, and I think he is due to play a Shield game soon."We're in a really good place. I think there was some unfair commentary around Steve in that last week. Perhaps I could have done a better job of trying to to soften that a bit. I think it probably got a little bit misconstrued how there was a level of disappointment in a such a big game that we were missing one of our great players. But no, we're very aligned going ahead. Very excited. He's very excited for the next 12 months. We'll need him. I'll need him, as captain, alongside me as vice-captain. So all very aligned."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: There were nine changes in the playing XIs as India and New Zealand made several changes for the fourth ODI of the five-match series at Mount Maunganui on Friday.New Zealand made six changes, while India brought in three players. India captain Shreyas Iyer won the toss and elected to bowl first.India are leading the series 2-0 after the third ODI in Hamilton was washed out due to rain.India bring in Gaikwad, Kishan and KuldeepAs expected, India handed opportunities to Ruturaj Gaikwad, Ishan Kishan and Kuldeep Yadav. Gaikwad will open the innings with Rohit Sharma after regular captain Shubman Gill was rested to prepare for the upcoming Test series.Kishan replaced KL Rahul, who will also join the team's preparations for the two-match Test series.Kuldeep Yadav was the third change in the Indian playing XI.Speaking at the toss, Iyer said India wanted to make the most of the conditions and treat the remaining matches as important contests."We will bowl first," Iyer said.Iyer said the possibility of dew later in the evening was one of the main reasons behind India's decision to bowl first."Yes, absolutely. I think it's about chasing, and when we looked at the wicket yesterday, there was a little bit amount of grass, but today it looks pretty dry, and also considering the dew coming in in the evening, one of the reasons we have opted to bowl first," Iyer said.With India leading the series 2-0, Iyer said the team would treat the fourth and fifth ODIs as knockout games.He also praised the team's approach despite the rain interruptions in the series."Well, it's important firstly to analyse the matches we've played before. We couldn't get proper games, but still I think the approach and attitude was phenomenal, and coming into this one, we are going to definitely treat it as a knockout. So the coming two games, it's going to be crucial and of cardinal importance," Iyer said.New Zealand make six changesNew Zealand made six changes to their playing XI, giving several players an opportunity to prove themselves.Nick Kelly, Dean Foxcroft, Finn Allen, Kristian Clarke, Michael Bracewell and Matt Henry came into the side.Captain Mitchell Santner said the changes would help New Zealand build their squad depth ahead of the World Cup year."Six changes.
