articles.title: IND vs NZ: Rohit Sharma, Ishan Kishan drop Will Young on consecutive deliveries to leave Auqib Nabi disappointed
articles.summary: First time was so nice, India had to do it twice.
articles.body: First time was so nice, India had to do it twice. New Zealand opener Will Young was given two lives in the space of two balls after Rohit Sharma and wicketkeeper Ishan Kishan dropped catches off consecutive deliveries in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday.The two chances came off the fifth and sixth balls of the second over, bowled by Auqib Nabi. Rohit was the first to put down a catch at first slip after Young edged a delivery outside off stump. Kishan then missed another opportunity behind the stumps off the very next ball, with Young getting another outside edge. Nabi was left disappointed as India failed to make the most of two early chances.Meanwhile, India may have a new captain, but their success at the toss has continued. Shreyas Iyer won the toss and elected to bowl in his first match as India's ODI captain. He took over from Shubman Gill, who has left the squad along with several other players to join India's Test team ahead of the first match against New Zealand, starting next Thursday.India have now won eight of the nine tosses across the T20I and ODI series, calling tails on every occasion.Ruturaj Gaikwad made his first appearance of the series, while Ishan Kishan took over wicketkeeping duties in place of KL Rahul. Kuldeep Yadav also returned to India's bowling line-up.New Zealand made several changes to their team due to injuries and players joining their Test squad. Nick Kelly, Dean Foxcroft and Finn Allen strengthened the batting line-up, while Kristian Clark and Matt Henry came into the pace attack.India lead the five-match series 2-0 and are in a position to become the first touring team in seven years to win an ODI series in New Zealand.Friday's match is also expected to avoid the rain interruptions that affected the earlier games. India won the rain-affected first ODI in Auckland by five wickets and the second in Wellington by four runs. articles.title: Time for some modifications as India aim to seal ODI series against New Zealand
articles.summary: With the Test series beginning on Nov 19, both India and New Zealand are having to juggle their resources, leaving their ODI combinations considerably
articles.body: With the Test series beginning on Nov 19, both India and New Zealand are having to juggle their resources, leaving their ODI combinations considerably different for the final two matches of the five-match series.Friday's fourth ODI at the Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui will see Shreyas Iyer take over the India captaincy, while New Zealand turn to a clutch of fresh faces as both teams look to find the right balance between immediate 50-over commitment and preparation for the longer format.The scheduling leaves the teams with little room for manoeuvring. The fifth and final ODI is on Nov 15, giving the players just three days before the opening Test in Wellington. Both camps have therefore split their resources, with several established players and members of the support staff moving to the Test set-up. The changes also present an opportunity to examine the depth of the ODI squads heading into the 2027 World Cup.India, who lead the five-match series 2-0 after the third ODI was washed out, will be looking to seal the contest. But the absence of regular skipper Shubman Gill, KL Rahul and Anshul Kamboj means the visitors will wear a different look. Iyer, who was Gill's deputy in the first three matches, will captain the side for the first time in ODIs. The batting order is likely to see some reshuffling. With Gill unavailable, it will be interesting to see who opens alongside Rohit Sharma. The options on that front are Ishan Kishan and Ruturaj Gaikwad, who has batted in the middle order in his last five ODI innings.Virat Kohli and Iyer provide the experience, while the availability of Tilak Varma gives India another option in the middle order. The team management will be keen to see how these combinations work, particularly with Kishan also expected to take over the wicketkeeping responsibilities in Rahul's absence.Iyer, meanwhile, has a personal challenge to address. He has struggled to get going in the series, with the extra bounce and seam movement in Auckland and Hamilton bringing his vulnerability against the short ball into focus. A change of conditions could offer some relief.Will Siraj get an opportunity?India's bowling combination will also be worth watching. With Kamboj having moved to the Test camp, Mohammed Siraj could get an opportunity to play in only his second international match since the tour of Sri Lanka in Aug. Arshdeep Singh, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi will shore up India's pace department. Also, Kuldeep Yadav remains available if India decide to go in with a frontline spinner. The decision will depend partly on the surface, which is expected to be more conducive to batting than the ones in the first two matches.New Zealand, on the other hand, have made several changes to their squad. Test captain Tom Latham, Daryl Mitchell, Glenn Phillips, Nathan Smith and Henry Nicholls have left for red-ball preparations, with Finn Allen, Mitch Hay, Dean Foxcroft, Nick Kelly and Brett Randell coming in. The hosts will have to rebuild parts of their batting order and find the right combination.The hosts will also hope the conditions allow their batters more freedom. The first two ODIs were played on seam-friendly surfaces, where the movement and bounce made run-scoring difficult. The weather forecast for Friday is clear, with no rain in the immediate lead-up to the match.New Zealand have already seen their 11-series winning streak at home in ODIs come to an end with defeats in the first two ODIs and the no-result in the third. They will now need to win both the remaining matches to avoid a series loss at home.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Seifert, on Thursday, said the different skills of Arshdeep Singh, Anshul Kamboj, Gurunoor Brar and Aqib Nabi had complemented each other effectively.“They all bring something different. Having Arshdeep as a left-armer is crucial as well. They have different qualities but they work well as a unit,” Seifert said, complimenting the attack’s ability to maintain discipline on surfaces that have offered a “good amount of assistance” to seamers. “To their credit, they didn’t miss much on those wickets in the first two games. Their consistency in hitting the right areas has made run-scoring difficult,” he said.Seifert was equally impressed by how India’s relatively inexperienced bowlers have adapted to the New Zealand conditions. “They’ve come to New Zealand and adapted to these wickets quickly. Hats off to them. At this level, you’ve to adapt to the conditions and the players you are up against, whether it’s Australia, England or India,” the opening batter said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Thought my chance would come in red-ball cricket first,' says Auqib Nabi
articles.summary: Red-ball cricket has been his calling card but it was the white ball that eventually brought Aqib Nabi his India breakthrough.
articles.body: Red-ball cricket has been his calling card but it was the white ball that eventually brought Aqib Nabi his India breakthrough. Having built his reputation through domestic performances in the longer format, the Jammu & Kashmir medium-pacer believed Test cricket would be his route into the national side. Instead, the selectors had a different plan, taking the 30-year-old by surprise.“I wasn’t expecting a white-ball call-up, to be honest. I thought my opportunity would come in red-ball cricket, in the Test format. But I see this (playing ODI cricket for India) as a great chance to showcase my skills,” Nabi said ahead of the fourth ODI between India and New Zealand.After a difficult ODI debut against the West Indies in Sept, where he conceded 84 runs without success on a flat Guwahati surface, Nabi has found conditions more to his liking in New Zealand. He has taken two wickets so far in his first four ODIs, both coming in India’s rain-affected victory in Wellington.In this short stint with the national team so far, there has also been a learning curve for Nabi. Bowling in New Zealand for the first time, he is focusing more on getting seam movement rather than conventional swing. “This is my first time bowling in New Zealand, so the conditions are a little different. You have to rely more on seam movement because top-level batters can play swing well. That was the feedback from Rohit bhai, Virat bhai and Shubman. If you bowl a scrambled-seam delivery or hit the deck hard, there is a greater chance of taking wickets here,” he said.‘Conditions similar to J&K’Interestingly, Nabi does not find the conditions entirely unfamiliar. The weather and surfaces in New Zealand, he believes, have similarities with those back home in Jammu & Kashmir. “The weather is quite similar because we experience comparable conditions back home as well. The main difference is the level of opposition. International cricket is different from domestic cricket, but the wickets are quite similar,” he said.The soft-spoken Nabi may not be blessed with express pace, but is confident that other attributes in his game can help him succeed at the highest level. “Of course, having extra pace is always an advantage. But I back my skills. I have performed well with them in domestic cricket, and I believe those strengths will help me at this level too,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: PLAYER OF THE MATCH - No prizes for guessing this one. It is Mahli Beardman who wins the award for his fantastic 6/24 on his debut. He describes his debut as an incredible day, admitting that the achievement is yet to fully sink in. He reveals that he goes to bed nervous but draws comfort from fond memories at the venue and the support of a wonderful group of teammates who help settle his nerves. Beardman says getting his first wicket is a huge relief, while Bison's leadership and the relaxed environment within the group make the transition to international cricket much easier. He also recalls Zampa advising him to keep a level head after that breakthrough and explains that he simply focuses on executing the team's plans. Reflecting on his journey back from a stress-related injury, Beardman admits there are occasional doubts but insists he never loses his love for the game. He adds that his way of switching off is to ignore the outside noise and, whenever time permits, head down to the beach for a swim.. Presentation Time.... Not enough runs on the board - England simply did not have enough runs on the board to make a contest of it. Gus Atkinson did offer a brief glimmer of hope with a wicket off his very first delivery, but that was quickly snuffed out by Bison's counter-attacking charge. Jofra Archer and Jamie Overton picked up a wicket apiece, but breakthroughs were few and far between, and England never really managed to put the hosts under any sustained pressure.. A quick chat - Australia's Spencer Johnson says that playing one-day cricket in Australia is always special. He praises Mahli Beardman for his energy and believes he has a bright future ahead. Johnson adds that it is an important series for the team and hopes they can make it 3-0. He also expresses his satisfaction at being able to perform and contribute to the team, acknowledging that injuries are part and parcel of sport. He hopes to stay fit and remain on the park for much longer.. A debut to remember for Beardman - Earlier in the game, England were bundled out for a paltry total after being asked to bat first, with debutant Mahli Beardman stealing the show with a sensational six-wicket haul. Tom Banton, Will Jacks and Gus Atkinson were the only batters to manage 25 or more, with the latter two sharing the highest partnership of just 37 in an otherwise dismal scorecard featuring six single-digit scores. Spencer Johnson also made a fine impact with 3/42, while Xavier Bartlett chipped in with a wicket.. Marsh fires as the Aussies cruise home - Chasing a modest target, Australia did suffer an early setback with Travis Head departing cheaply, but Mitchell Marsh ensured there was no shift in momentum. Carrying his rich vein of form from South Africa, he went on a spectacular hitting spree, racing to a 29-ball half-century and putting England's bowlers under immense pressure. His 61-run partnership with Connolly effectively broke the back of the chase, although both batters fell shortly after Marsh reached his milestone. articles.title: Joe Root scripts history against Australia, becomes only third England player to enter elite 200 list
articles.summary: England batting mainstay Joe Root on Friday became only the third player from the country to feature in 200 One-Day Internationals (ODIs).
articles.body: England batting mainstay Joe Root on Friday became only the third player from the country to feature in 200 One-Day Internationals (ODIs). Root reached the milestone when he took the field for the first ODI against Australia at Perth Stadium.He joined Eoin Morgan, who played 225 ODIs, and Jos Buttler, who has 204 appearances, in the list of England players to reach the landmark.Australia captain Mitch Marsh won the toss and elected to bowl in the series opener, which comes amid renewed attention on the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal. Less than four hours before the toss, Australia Test captain Pat Cummins addressed a news conference in Sydney, dismissing claims made in Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, released this week, as “complete and utter nonsense.”Marsh said the opening ODI of the three-match series would be an important start to a busy 12 months for Australia, which includes a home Test series against New Zealand, tours of India and England, and next year's World Cup in South Africa.“It’s the start of the summer for us (and) that first game is always important,” he said.Australia will be without several of their first-choice fast bowlers for the white-ball series, with Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Scott Boland missing from the squad. Xavier Bartlett, left-arm pacer Spencer Johnson and 21-year-old Mahli Beardman are part of the bowling attack instead.Beardman, who hails from Western Australia, is making his international debut. Marsh said the young fast bowler would have a special occasion playing his first international match at home.“It’s going to be exciting for him. No better place in the world for a young West Australian to debut,” Marsh said. “We've got a reasonably young and inexperienced side, but lots of energy.”Australia are playing their first ODI since September, when they lost a three-match series 2-1 against South Africa.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Threw Usman Khawaja under the bus': David Warner hits out at Pat Cummins over sandpaper row - WATCH
articles.summary: Former Australia opener David Warner has continued to back Usman Khawaja following his explosive claims about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, also known
articles.body: Former Australia opener David Warner has continued to back Usman Khawaja following his explosive claims about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, also known as Sandpapergate. A few hours after Australia captain Pat Cummins addressed the allegations at a news conference in Sydney, Warner accused him of throwing Khawaja under the bus.Warner, who was handed a 12-month ban for his role in the 2018 scandal, backed Khawaja's version of events in his autobiography, Sabr. Khawaja has claimed that all members of the Test team knew about the use of sandpaper during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.This contradicts Cummins' public statements. The current Australia captain has repeatedly denied knowing about the sandpaper plot.Speaking on Fox Cricket's coverage of Australia's first ODI against England at Optus Stadium in Perth, Warner made his support for Khawaja clear.“I still stick by Uzzie,” he said.“And what he's written in that in that book. It is the truth and I really, really support him.“I actually feel for him at the moment. I actually feel that the captain today actually threw Uzzie under the bus. And I'm very, very disappointed about that.”Warner also repeated his criticism of the investigation into the scandal, describing it as "botched."Cummins calls Khawaja's claims 'complete and utter nonsense'Cummins held a news conference at the Sydney Cricket Ground on Friday, hours before Australia's home-season opening ODI against England in Perth.He said he was ready to answer questions for as long as required because he wanted to put the controversy behind him.Khawaja's autobiography has brought the eight-year-old scandal back into the spotlight. In the book, he claimed that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering plan.Cummins, who was part of Australia's bowling attack in the Cape Town Test, strongly rejected the claim.“When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100% wrong,” Cummins said. “I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.“But I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense.”What happened in the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal?The controversy erupted during Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town in March 2018. Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera using sandpaper on the ball.Following a Cricket Australia investigation, three players received bans. Then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain Warner were suspended for 12 months, while Bancroft received a nine-month ban.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Virat Kohli plays peacemaker after Gurnoor Brar's animated send-off to Seifert, video goes viral - Watch
articles.summary: India pacer Gurnoor Brar made the first breakthrough in the fourth ODI against New Zealand at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday, dismissing opener Tim
articles.body: India pacer Gurnoor Brar made the first breakthrough in the fourth ODI against New Zealand at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday, dismissing opener Tim Seifert in the 12th over. However, it was his reaction after taking the wicket that grabbed attention, with Virat Kohli stepping in to calm down the young fast bowler.Seifert attempted to pull Brar off the sixth ball of the 12th over but failed to make proper contact. The ball went high in the air and wicketkeeper Ishan Kishan completed the catch.The New Zealand opener scored 58 off 48 balls, hitting six fours and three sixes. His dismissal also ended the 85-run opening partnership with Will Young.Brar had been involved in a verbal exchange with Seifert earlier in the innings as the New Zealand batter took on India's new-ball bowlers. The pacer had also been hit for a four by Seifert shortly before the dismissal.After getting the wicket, Brar walked towards Seifert and gave him an animated send-off, getting close to the batter as he celebrated. Seifert appeared unhappy with the reaction and looked ready to confront the Indian pacer.However, Kohli stepped in and pulled Brar away, preventing the exchange from escalating. Several videos of the incident have since surfaced on social media, with Kohli seen calming down his young teammate.The incident also caught the attention of the on-air commentators, who expressed surprise at Kohli taking on the role of peacemaker, considering his own history of animated exchanges with opposition players.Earlier, stand-in India captain Shreyas Iyer won the toss and elected to field in the fourth ODI. Brar was included in India's three-man pace attack for the match.Will Young scored his first century against India in ODIs as New Zealand finished at 333 in 50 overs in the first innings.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IND vs NZ 4th ODI: Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Shreyas Iyer fall for ducks; India suffer first-ever 0/3 start in ODIs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India suffered a shocking start to their chase of 334 against New Zealand in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India suffered a shocking start to their chase of 334 against New Zealand in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday. Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and captain Shreyas Iyer all returned to the pavilion without scoring. New Zealand pacer Matt Henry dismissed all three batters in the opening over to leave India reeling at 0/3.Henry opened the bowling for New Zealand and struck with his very first delivery. He then removed Kohli on the fifth ball before sending Iyer back on the final delivery of the over.It was a triple-wicket maiden for Henry, who gave New Zealand the perfect start after the hosts had posted 333.Rohit falls for a golden duckHenry got Rohit Sharma with the first ball of the innings. The New Zealand pacer bowled a short-of-a-good-length delivery that moved away from the right-hander and also produced extra bounce. Rohit was forced to play at it and got a thick outside edge. Finn Allen took a simple catch at first slip. Rohit walked back after facing just one ball, registering a golden duck.Rohit Sharma c Finn Allen b Matt Henry 0 (1)Henry cleans up KohliHenry struck again on the fifth ball of the over to remove Virat Kohli. After bowling deliveries that moved away from the batter, Henry brought one back sharply into Kohli. The ball stayed a little low as Kohli tried to defend it towards the leg-side.Kohli was unable to deal with the inward movement. The ball went through the gap between his bat and pad and hit the stumps. Kohli was bowled for a four-ball duck, leaving India at 0/2.Virat Kohli b Matt Henry 0 (4)Shreyas Iyer falls LBW on the final ballHenry completed a stunning over by dismissing India captain Shreyas Iyer on the final delivery. The pacer bowled a sharp delivery that came back into Iyer. The batter tried to defend it but missed the ball, which hit him on the back leg.Umpire Kumar Dharmasena initially turned down the appeal. New Zealand took a review, and ball-tracking showed three reds, confirming that the ball would have hit the middle stump.Iyer was given out LBW for a first-ball duck. Henry had completed a triple-wicket maiden, with India losing their first three wickets without scoring a run.Shreyas Iyer lbw b Matt Henry 0 (1)Rohit and Kohli register second ODI ducks togetherThis was only the second time that Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli had both scored ducks in the same ODI.The previous instance came against Sri Lanka in Dambulla in 2010. That match is also remembered for the controversial incident in which Virender Sehwag was denied a century after Suraj Randiv bowled a no-ball when Sehwag was on 99 not out. Sehwag hit the delivery for six, but the run did not count.India join unwanted ODI record listIndia became the fifth team to lose their first three wickets without scoring a run in an ODI.The previous instances were:Pakistan vs New Zealand, Edgbaston, 1983 World CupPakistan vs South Africa, Lahore, 1997Bangladesh vs Sri Lanka, Pietermaritzburg, 2003 World CupAustralia vs Bangladesh, Mirpur, 2026India vs New Zealand, Mount Maunganui, 2026Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'What's just happened': Mahli Beardman does what McGrath, Starc and Cummins couldn't; Aussie pacer unleashes pace storm on debut against England to make history
articles.summary: Australia's 21-year-old pacer Mahli Beardman made a dream start to his international career, tearing through England's batting line-up to claim six
articles.body: Australia's 21-year-old pacer Mahli Beardman made a dream start to his international career, tearing through England's batting line-up to claim six wickets on his ODI debut in Perth on Friday. With figures of 6/24, Beardman became the first Australian male fast bowler to take a six-wicket haul on ODI debut, breaking a record that had stood for 38 years.Beardman also became only the second Australian male bowler to take five or more wickets in his first ODI as England were bowled out for just 131 in the series opener.The young pacer struck early, removing England captain Harry Brook before sending Joe Root back to the pavilion. His double blow left England struggling at 55/4 after 14 overs on the Perth Stadium pitch.Beardman continued to trouble the visitors, adding the wickets of Jordan Cox, Sam Curran, Liam Dawson and Jofra Archer to complete his six-wicket haul. The former Australia Under-19 World Cup player thus surpassed the record held by Tony Dodemaide, who had taken five wickets on his ODI debut against Sri Lanka on January 2, 1988, at the WACA in Perth.Dodemaide had returned figures of 5/21 in 7.2 overs in that match, a record that remained untouched for 38 years.Beardman's figures of 6/24 are now the best by an Australian male bowler on ODI debut and the fourth-best overall in men's cricket. Only Charlie Cassell of Scotland, Kagiso Rabada of South Africa and Fidel Edwards of the West Indies have recorded better figures on their ODI debuts.Speaking to Australia great Mike Hussey during the innings break after claiming his sixth wicket, Beardman admitted that he had been nervous before the match."I'm not sure what's just happened," Beardman said."It all happened very quickly but it's just a great honour to represent my country and to take a few wickets is the cherry on top."I was pretty nervous early. First ball just trying to hit the cut stuff. Once that got out the way everything started to feel natural."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Young was dropped twice in the second over of New Zealand's innings. Rohit Sharma missed a chance at first slip off Auqib Nabi, and wicketkeeper Ishan Kishan then failed to hold on to the next delivery.Young was batting on just five at the time. He made full use of the two lifelines, scoring 125 off 88 balls to register his fifth ODI century. It was also his first hundred against India and his highest score in the format.The right-hander had managed just nine runs in the first ODI and six in the second. The third match was abandoned due to rain.After his dismissal, Young spoke about the two dropped catches and revealed a funny conversation with Virat Kohli.Young's chat with Kohli after two dropped catchesYoung admitted that he was disappointed after the first dropped catch but was relieved to get another chance. The second miss left him laughing."Well, the first one, obviously a little bit disappointed, but at the same time relieved. The second one, you just got to laugh it off. Virat came up to me and I said, "Have you ever been dropped twice in an over?" He laughs and said no, so just brush it off and next ball."Young also explained how he changed his batting approach after getting those two lifelines."Yeah, I did actually notice that I was a little bit stuck on the crease after that, those two drops. I decided to walk at them and get my weight through the ball a bit more, and that seemed to work in my favour."'A little bit of relief': Young on his centuryYoung said he was relieved to spend time at the crease and convert his start into a big score."A little bit of relief, firstly, but no, it's been amazing to spend some time in the middle. Obviously a little bit of fortune early in my innings, but I managed to stick at it and put a decent score together with a few partnerships in the middle."Young credits partnerships for New Zealand's 333Young also spoke about the contributions of his fellow batters, including opening partner Tim Seifert. He said New Zealand's total was built through a series of partnerships."I try to enjoy myself the whole time. Obviously, having Seifert at the other end in the opening partnership was brilliant. He played really well, and I think it was just a story of small partnerships throughout the innings, which got us to that 333. When Finn came to the middle, he talked about enjoying it and playing with a smile on his face, so that was great to see too."Is 333 enough for New Zealand?Young felt New Zealand had hoped to score a few more runs but was happy with the final total after losing wickets at regular intervals."Yeah, I think at a certain stage in the innings we would have liked a little bit more, but we did keep losing wickets. So to scrap through to 333 I think is a decent score. Obviously it might be a little bit easier chasing, but I think stats say that 314 is the average first innings winning score. So hopefully that's enough. Early wickets, feel like demons, hopefully it is."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: England in Australia: Mahli Beardman takes six wickets as England thrashed
articles.summary: England meekly offer Australia respite from the ongoing sandpaper scandal by being bowled out for 131 in the first one-day international in Perth.
articles.body:
England 131 (33.4 overs): Atkinson 29*; Beardman 6-24

Australia 132-3 (23.3 overs): Marsh 50, Connolly 27

England meekly offered Australia respite from the ongoing sandpaper scandal by being bowled out for 131 in a seven-wicket thrashing in the first one-day international in Perth.

Hours after Pat Cummins emphatically hit back at Usman Khawaja's comments , Harry Brook's England folded as 21-year-old fast bowler Mahli Beardman emerged with a stunning 6-24 on his ODI debut.

Beardman nicked off Brook in his second over for his first international wicket. Less than two hours later, bowling accurately and at good pace, he had the best figures by an Australian on ODI debut.

His second ODI wicket was the prized scalp of Joe Root for 17 and he also dismissed Tom Banton, whose 25 was one of only three scores over 20, Jordan Cox and Sam Curran in an opening spell of five overs that returned figures of 5-18.

Ben Duckett, Banton and Root, plus Beardman's later victims Liam Dawson and Jofra Archer, fell driving in Perth – dismissals familiar from England's wretched start to last winter's Ashes series on the same ground.

This was another Perth surface offering pace and bounce and England had no answer.

Talk of the sandpaper scandal still swirls around the game - the day began with David Warner accusing Cummins of throwing Khawaja "under the bus" on the Australian TV coverage - but England missed the chance to apply more misery to their oldest foe.

Captain Mitchell Marsh, who repeatedly dodged questions about ball tampering in his news conference on Thursday, thrashed a 29-ball fifty as Australia chased their target with a massive 26.3 overs to spare.

The second of three ODIs is on Sunday in Adelaide (03:30 GMT) with England, who suffered damaging defeats in the tri-series against Pakistan and Sri Lanka last month, desperately needing a response as they attempt to build towards next year's World Cup after four defeats in their past five matches.

England floundering in Perth? You'd be forgiven for thinking you were back in 2025. Next week marks a year since the last Ashes began.

On that occasion, and after minimal preparation, batters were guilty of driving on the up and gifting their wickets.

The openers here - Banton getting a thick edge to a drive with his feet planted and Duckett slicing left-armer Spencer Johnson to backward point - were eerily familiar. England have had lengthy build-up here. That is no excuse this time.

In fairness to Brook, he got a good ball from Beardman which was fiddled behind. Root's ball was of driving length, but he got a thick edge.

Cox then tentatively nicked off from the crease for two and Curran's issues against the short ball were laid bare when he top-edged a hook to fine leg off Beardman, who exceeded 90mph at times, for a seven-ball duck.

From 65-8, Will Jacks offered brief resistance with 25 and Gus Atkinson hit the innings' only six for 29 not out. England were still dismissed inside 34 overs - the 15th time they have been bowled out in 29 ODIs since Brendon McCullum took over as coach. Eleven of those instances have come when batting first.

"England are trying," former England captain Michael Vaughan said on Test Match Special.

"It's not what it was a year ago when the message was just 'we'll just go harder and, if we get bowled out, we'll go harder the next time'.

"I didn't see that today but what I saw were some basic errors on the pitch they're playing on and for this side to become a side that can win the World Cup in a year, they need to improve quickly."

The win will not banish all talk of sandpaper in Australia but at least provided a distraction.

It is unlikely Beardman would be playing in this series had Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood – the three fast bowlers whose role in Cape Town has been pushed back into the spotlight by Khawaja's new book – not been rested.

Now front and centre after a young career hampered by back injuries, Beardman hinted at what future could await when those three iconic bowlers do retire.

Using the life the pitch offered, he threatened with full balls and short, and bowled an ideal line. Xavier Bartlett, 27, was also impressive with the new ball while Johnson added the wickets of Jamie Overton and Jacks after the scalp of Duckett.

Travis Head, who put England to the sword in the Perth chase a year ago, dragged on for a first-ball duck. Australia's chase was still a formality.

Like Head before him, Marsh flogged the bowling, looking far more comfortable than England on his home ground when clubbing four sixes over the leg side.

"Batting here with extra pace and bounce you need to invest a bit more in the early part of your innings," former Australia all-rounder Tom Moody said. "You don't have to leave every ball, but be a bit more mindful.

"England didn't make the assessment and make the adjustment to be productive. I'm not saying it's a 300 surface, but you would be disappointed with something between 230 or 250.

"There was a consistent theme in their whole innings where they were pushing at length balls which were bouncing and moving away."

After Marsh holed out for 50 and Cooper Connolly 27, Josh Inglis and Matthew Renshaw calmly steered Australia to their win.

They took their time but only twice before had they beaten England with as many balls to spare.

'We talked extensively about the conditions'

England coach Brendon McCullum, speaking to TNT Sports: "It all happened pretty quickly. I thought we weren't quick enough to adapt to the conditions, we talked extensively leading into the game about the surface here at Optus is a bit like batting on a trampoline, there's certain shots that are obviously very difficult to try and execute and we talked a lot about trying to put those away.

"And also looking at some of the history of the games here as well, the last four games have all been over in 30-odd overs. So we knew we were probably in for a bit of a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.

"Overall, obviously disappointed, but there's some good lessons in it for us as well. If you look towards the World Cup and South Africa there's going to be some pitches there that may not have quite the same bounce as this but will definitely test us from a bounce point of you. And we'll have to find ways to be able to counter that and we'll have those conversations."

articles.title: IND vs NZ 4th ODI: 9/4 again! Team India suffer 1983 World Cup deja vu after 43 years
articles.summary: India's batting collapse against New Zealand brought back memories of one of the most famous moments in their cricket history.
articles.body: India's batting collapse against New Zealand brought back memories of one of the most famous moments in their cricket history. Forty-three years after being reduced to 9/4 against Zimbabwe in the 1983 World Cup, India suffered the same score in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday.Chasing 334, India lost their first three wickets without scoring a run. Matt Henry struck with the very first ball of the innings, dismissing Rohit Sharma, before removing Virat Kohli and captain Shreyas Iyer in the same over.Rohit was caught by Finn Allen at first slip, Kohli was bowled while trying to defend a delivery that came back in, and Iyer was trapped LBW after New Zealand successfully reviewed the decision.The damage did not stop there. Ruturaj Gaikwad was dismissed for five, leaving India struggling at 9/4.Same score after 43 yearsThe 1983 World Cup match against Zimbabwe at Tunbridge Wells is remembered for Kapil Dev's remarkable 175 not out. India were in deep trouble at 17/5 before their captain produced one of the greatest innings in World Cup history to rescue the team.On Friday, India were once again reduced to 9/4. It was only the second time that India had lost their first four wickets for fewer than 10 runs in an ODI. The first instance was the famous collapse against Zimbabwe in 1983.India's lowest scores in first 10 overs since 2018India's 26/4 in the first 10 overs against New Zealand was their lowest score in this period since 2018.Here are India's lowest scores in the first 10 overs of ODIs since 2018:21/3 against Australia in Sydney, 201922/4 against New Zealand in Wellington, 201924/4 against New Zealand at Old Trafford in the 2019 World Cup24/2 against South Africa in Lucknow, 202226/1 against Australia in Melbourne, 201926/4 against New Zealand in Mount Maunganui, 2026Henry has troubled India in previous matches too. He took 2/10 in Wellington in 2019 and 3/13 against India at Old Trafford during the 2019 World Cup. On Friday, he took 3/14 during India's early collapse.Rohit and Kohli register ducks together for only the second timeRohit and Kohli both failed to open their accounts against New Zealand. It was only the second time in their ODI careers that both had been dismissed for zero in the same match.The first instance came against Sri Lanka in Dambulla in 2010. The second was on Friday in Mount Maunganui.Matt Henry's record against Rohit and KohliHenry has dismissed both Rohit and Kohli three times in ODIs. Rohit has scored 57 runs off 71 balls against the New Zealand pacer, averaging 19 at a strike rate of 80.28.Kohli has made 59 runs off 60 balls against Henry. He averages 19.67, with a strike rate of 98.33.Rohit joins list of Indian batters dismissed off the first ballRohit was out on the first ball of India's innings. He became only the latest Indian batter to suffer this dismissal. Sourav Ganguly and Virender Sehwag hold the unwanted record of being dismissed off the first ball of an ODI innings three times each.Sunil Gavaskar, Ravi Shastri, Kris Srikkanth, Manoj Prabhakar and Rohit have suffered the same fate once each.Teams to lose their first three wickets without scoring in ODIsIndia also joined a list of teams that have lost their first three wickets without putting a run on the board in an ODI.The previous instances were:Pakistan vs New Zealand, Edgbaston, 1983 World CupPakistan vs South Africa, Lahore, 1997Bangladesh vs Sri Lanka, Pietermaritzburg, 2003 World CupAustralia vs Bangladesh, Mirpur, 2026India vs New Zealand, Mount Maunganui, 2026Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body:
Scotland 111-8 (20 overs): Carter 62; Masqood 3-18

Scotland succumbed to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy campaign Group A fixture.

Having opened with victory over Papua New Guinea, the Scots batted first against Sri Lanka but were restricted to 111-8 in Ajman, United Arab Emirates.

Darcey Carter top scored on 62 runs off 55 deliveries while Sathya Sandeepani and Sugandika Kumari took two wickets each.

Sri Lanka's Vishmi Gunaratne amassed 49 runs off 41 deliveries, with captain Harshitha Samarawickrama contributing 24.

Abatha Masqood took three wickets, becoming the Scots' top wicket taker in WT20Is, her 77 surpassing current captain Kathryn Bryce.

Ten nations are participating in the UAE, split into two groups of five before a Super Six stage to determine the final on 25 November.

Scotland play the hosts next, with UAE having opened with defeat by Ireland, who picked up a first win.

articles.title: Pat Cummins: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back, reopening wounds in a 'nation of good sports'
articles.summary: Claims the entire Australian team knew of the 2018 sandpaper cheating plot are dividing the cricket world.
articles.body:
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.

Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.

"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."

A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.

Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."

"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.

There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.

"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.

"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."

Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.

In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.

"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."

However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.

David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.

But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.

And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.

Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".

"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.

"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."

He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.

He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.

"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.

Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.

"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."

"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.

"I don't know what the outcome will be."

articles.title: England crumble against Australia in Perth again as Mitchell Marsh's side win first ODI amid 'Sandpapergate' storm
articles.summary: England wilt to 131 all out as Australia take 1-0 lead in three-match ODI series on day Pat Cummins launches stunning response to Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' claims; seamer Mahli Beardman, 21, takes best figures by an Australia bowler on ODI debut, including Harry Brook and Joe Root
articles.body:
England's raft of rash strokes in last November's first Ashes Test at Optus Stadium led to them losing that game inside two days en route to a harrowing 4-1 series defeat.

Unlike the previous winter, the tourists played a proper warm-up game at another Perth venue in The WACA, beating a Western Australia side by 92 runs last Saturday as 21-year-old pacer Beardman went wicketless from 10 overs.

Fast forward six days and Beardman bagged the best figures by an Australian on ODI debut - his 6-24 from 7.4 overs topping Tony Dodemaide's 5-21 versus Sri Lanka in 1988 - with his five-for on his home ground coming in 28 balls as England slumped to 132 all out, a total Australia eclipsed in 23.3 overs.

Harry Brook (1), who became Beardman's first wicket when he poked behind in the 12th over, saw his side bundled out in just 33.4 overs with Joe Root (17), playing his 200th ODI, one of a number of players to perish on the drive, the sort of shot that had got England in all sorts of bother during their Test trouncing here a year ago.

Brook's men rallied somewhat from 65-8, passing their lowest-ever ODI score of 86 and reaching three figures thanks to Will Jacks (25) and Gus Atkinson, who top-scored with 29 not out from 32 balls from the No 10 spot and hit England's sole six.

But a target of 132 was never likely to trouble Australia, despite Atkinson bowling Travis Head - who had slammed a match-winning hundred in that Ashes clash in Perth in 2025 - for a golden duck in the second over and so it proved, as stand-in captain Mitchell Marsh tonked a 29-ball fifty before holing out with 65 runs needed.

Marsh's eight-boundary onslaught (four sixes, four fours) came a day after dead-batting all questions about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in Cape Town, which has been catapulted back onto the news agenda following the release of Usman Khawaja's book.

Beardman the star after Cummins hogs the headlines

Marsh is leading Australia in this three-match series in place of the rested Pat Cummins - but the latter was, along with Beardman, the undoubted story of Friday as he held an extraordinary, 68-minute press conference to address Khawaja's comments.

Cummins insisted Khawaja's claims that every member of the Baggy Greens dressing room back then was aware of the plot to alter the ball using sandpaper to be "100 per cent untrue" and "utter nonsense" before lauding "really exciting prospect" Beardman.

As fans and media digested Cummins' startling response to Khawaja's accusations, a couple of hours later they were hailing Beardman's record-breaking ODI bow, where he displayed accuracy, speed and skill and offered a glimpse into the future.

The seamer nicked off Brook, Root and Jordan Cox (2), bounced out Sam Curran (0), had Liam Dawson - once again preferred in the England XI to fellow spinner Adil Rashid - caught at backward point for a duck and ended the innings when last man Jofra Archer (11) was athletically pouched by a diving Jack Edwards in the gully.

An Australia attack missing Cummins and two other rested fast-bowling stalwarts in Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazelwood excelled with left-armer Spencer Johnson's 3-42 including Ben Duckett (9) caught square driving to backward point after England lost the toss and new-ball partner Xavier Bartlett (1-46) removing Tom Banton (25).

England took a few scalps in the chase in Head, Marsh and Cooper Connolly (27 off 30) but Australia eased to victory and will now look to wrap up a series win with a game to spare in Adelaide on Sunday ahead of next Wednesday's final game in Hobart.

Brook's team are not at full strength - they are shorn of the injured Jacob Bethell (knee), Jos Buttler (hamstring) and Josh Tongue (toe) - but neither are Australia, so this defeat, following swiftly on from their tri-series travails in Pakistan last month when they lost three of their four matches, leaves England with plenty to ponder.

Beardman 'outstanding' but England didn't 'execute well enough'

England captain Harry Brook, speaking at the presentation:

"We have been in Perth for a week and a half and prepared extremely well [but] Australia bowled extremely well.

"Beardman was outstanding. He put the ball in the right areas and got enough out of the surface to dismiss us.

"We have spoken a lot about adaptability. We want to adapt to different surfaces and we knew certain shots weren't going to work on this pitch. We probably didn't execute our skills well enough.

"The bigger picture is that there is a World Cup in South Africa in 12 months' time and these experiences - we try to bank them and learn from them as much as we can. We are not out of this series."

'I would love to live my life like Beardman'

Australia captain Mitchell Marsh, on Mahli Beardman:

"He is a fantastic young kid - I would love to live my life like him: carefree, loves the ocean, loves learning about fast bowling.

"He has had a few injury problems but he is a really confident, gentle young man.

"I had nothing but a smile on my face seeing that today. Whether or not he took wickets, he brings a certain energy and it is a fantastic start to his career.

"Mahli's already said he's not sure who is coming back in for him, so the big three [Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood] might have a sleepless night.

"There's some really good talent around the country, a lot of fast bowling talent, which is really exciting."

Second ODI: Sunday November 15 (Adelaide)

Third ODI: Wednesday November 18 (Hobart)

First T20I: Saturday November 21 (Melbourne)

Second T20I: Tuesday November 24 (Carrara)

Third T20I: Friday November 27 (Brisbane)

Fourth T20I: Sunday November 29 (Sydney)

Fifth T20I: Wednesday December 2 (Canberra)

articles.title: Matt Henry vs India: A familiar storyline awakens ghosts of the past
articles.summary: MOUNT MAUNGANUI: Seagulls began circling the Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui in full force just as India were about to begin their run chase.
articles.body: MOUNT MAUNGANUI: Seagulls began circling the Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui in full force just as India were about to begin their run chase. Little did they know that they would soon be joined by flying ducks as Matt Henry ran through the visitors' top order, dismissing Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer in the very first over of India's innings.Henry needed just six deliveries to awaken the ghosts of the 2019 World Cup semifinal, sending back three right-handers for ducks. The only consolation for India seven years ago was that their top three -- KL Rahul, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli -- had at least managed to score one run each.Chasing 334, India lost Rohit off the first ball. Rohit closed his bat face a bit early and was squared up, Kohli was cleaned up by a sharp in-dipper that kept a tad low, and India's stand-in skipper Iyer had no response to a delivery that jagged back sharply after pitching. Using his magic length and dangerous wobble seam, Henry put India on the mat in the very first over. Spectators who had stepped out for a quick hydration and refuelling break were shocked when they looked at the scoreline on the giant screen, and some even started walking out with disappointment written all over their faces.They had come hoping to witness special knocks from Kohli and Rohit but would have to make peace with the long walks back to the dressing room. And before they could settle back into their respective chairs or on the grass banks, Iyer joined the duck parade. Matters could have been worse had Nick Kelly held on to a regulation catch offered by Axar Patel off the first delivery he faced. Seeing Henry breathe fire, Kyle Jamieson soon joined the hunting pack, getting rid of Ruturaj Gaikwad as India lost four wickets inside the first 10 overs.Henry was not done. He returned to the attack and struck immediately, ending Ishan Kishan's resistance with his very first delivery. Bowling from round the wicket, the New Zealand pacer got one to jag back sharply from a good length. Ishan moved forward to defend but left a gap between bat and pad. The inside edge ricocheted onto the leg-stump, clipping the bail and ending his innings. The 34-year-old completed his five-wicket haul, his fourth in ODIs, with another display of his trademark nagging line and length and a hint of inward movement. Henry got the ball to nip back in sharply. Kuldeep Yadav was late in getting forward, allowing the delivery to beat his inside edge and defence before crashing into the top of the off-stump.Matt Henry finished with his career-best figures of 6/27 as New Zealand hammered India by 244 runs.This was the third time India had suffered this unwanted feat in ODIs since 2018, and all three instances featured the common wreaker-in-chief: Henry. The fast bowler picked up two wickets when India lost four in Wellington in 2019, three during the World Cup semifinal at Old Trafford the same year, and continued with his habit at the Bay Oval.The pitch didn't change drastically when twilight set in, but the evening chill injected just enough life into the surface, which had looked very comfortable for batting during New Zealand's innings. More than the surface, Henry found the right spot from the word go and stuck to it with his wobble seam. The two turned out to be a deadly combination, yet again, and made India join the list of several unwanted firsts.This was only the second time both Kohli and Rohit had registered ducks in an ODI and the first instance in which India lost three wickets without adding anything to the scoreboard. It had happened only four times earlier in the history of one-day cricket.India would hope to forget those six deliveries like a horror dream and bounce back strongly when they return to the same venue for the fixture that will decide the series."45 minutes of bad cricket (in Kohli's words)" against an attack featuring the usual suspect, Henry, had "cost" India the semifinal back in 2019. This time, it took Henry only a few minutes to stamp his authority in a series he had missed due to a freak injury. The eventful over nicely sets up the final match and the Test series that follows. Henry vs India remains a very interesting storyline.Brief ScoresNew Zealand: 333 all out in 50 overs (Will Young 125, Finn Allen 41; Axar Patel 2/39, Auqib Nabi 2/59, Gurnoor Brar 2/69)India: 89 all out in 26.4 overs (Ishan Kishan 27; Matt Henry 6/27, Matthew Fisher 3/31)Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: India suffered their second-biggest defeat by runs in one-day internationals after New Zealand beat them by 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval in
articles.body: India suffered their second-biggest defeat by runs in one-day internationals after New Zealand beat them by 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday.Chasing 334 for victory, India were bowled out for just 89, with New Zealand pacer Matt Henry taking six wickets. Will Young led the hosts' batting effort with a century as they registered a dominant win.India still lead the five-match series 2-1. New Zealand cannot win the series but can level it by winning the final match at the same venue on Sunday. The third ODI was abandoned due to rain.India's second-biggest defeat in ODIsIndia's 244-run defeat is now the second-biggest by runs in their ODI history. Their heaviest loss came against Sri Lanka, who beat them by 245 runs in Sharjah in 2000. The defeat against New Zealand is just one run short of that unwanted record.India's other biggest defeats include a 214-run loss to South Africa in Mumbai in 2015 and a 208-run defeat against Australia in Sydney in 2004.Biggest defeat margins for India in ODIs:245 runs vs Sri Lanka, Sharjah, 2000244 runs vs New Zealand, Mount Maunganui, 2026214 runs vs South Africa, Mumbai WS, 2015208 runs vs Australia, Sydney, 2004202 runs vs England, Lord’s, World Cup 1975200 runs vs New Zealand, Dambulla, 2010Henry's first-over burst leaves India in troubleIndia's chase got off to a disastrous start as Henry struck three times in the opening over. He dismissed Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer to leave India reeling at 0/3.Ruturaj Gaikwad also fell soon after, leaving India in deep trouble. Ishan Kishan (27) and Axar Patel (21) then put together a 44-run partnership, while Naman Dhir added a quick 21.Their efforts helped India avoid an even bigger defeat. Henry returned to take three more wickets and finished with six as India were bowled out for their sixth-lowest total in ODIs.Young makes up for early failures with a centuryEarlier, Young produced a fine innings of 125 off 108 balls to give New Zealand a strong total. It was his highest ODI score and his fifth century in the format.The 33-year-old had managed only nine and six in the first two matches of the series. He made the most of his chances after India dropped him twice in the second over, with Rohit and wicketkeeper Kishan putting down catches off consecutive deliveries.Young received good support from Tim Seifert, who scored 58, and Finn Allen, who made 41. For India, Axar Patel, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi took two wickets each.Gill, Rahul miss final ODI tooIndia were without captain Shubman Gill and batter KL Rahul for the fourth ODI. articles.summary: India's stand-in captain Shreyas Iyer admitted that New Zealand's bowling made the difference after the visitors suffered a humiliating 244-run defeat in
articles.body: India's stand-in captain Shreyas Iyer admitted that New Zealand's bowling made the difference after the visitors suffered a humiliating 244-run defeat in the fourth ODI at Bay Oval, Mount Maunganui, on Friday.Chasing 334, India were bowled out for just 89 in 28.4 overs, with Matt Henry producing a sensational six-wicket haul to dismantle the batting order. The defeat reduced India's lead in the five-match series to 2-1, with the third ODI having been washed out.Speaking after the match, Iyer acknowledged the impact of Henry's opening spell and credited the New Zealand pacer for consistently bowling in the right areas."We saw it, there was a huge difference in the first innings and the second innings in terms of wicket, but also credit where it's due, the way Henry bowled in the right areas right from ball one. I think that was sensational," Iyer said.Iyer defends India's batting performanceIndia's batting collapse began in the opening over when Henry dismissed Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer, leaving the visitors reeling at 0/3. Iyer admitted that India had tried different bowling strategies during New Zealand's innings but struggled to contain the hosts. He also pointed to missed opportunities in the field, while acknowledging that the team expected to chase the target comfortably after watching New Zealand score 333."I think we tried almost everything in the first innings, the way they were playing on the rise. And we thought that the wicket was better to bat on considering they got 330 after that. Obviously a couple of dropped catches, but that definitely happens in a game," he said.The Indian captain also defended his batters, insisting that they were dismissed by quality deliveries rather than throwing their wickets away."But yeah, when we got into the dressing room, we thought that we would be cruising through the chase as well. But the way the ball was seaming in and out, you couldn't basically decide from inside that this is how I'm going to play. Or even if you saw the wickets, no one threw the wicket away. It was good deliveries," Iyer added.Shreyas Iyer urges India to move onDespite the heavy defeat, Iyer reminded his teammates that India had won the first two matches and urged them to take confidence from those performances ahead of the series decider."It's important to forget about this one, obviously, analyze what went wrong in terms of bowling and batting. But at the back of the mind it's important that we have also won two games. So a lot of inspiration from that one and see to it that we come with a fresh set of mind," he said.New Zealand had earlier posted 333, powered by Will Young's 125 off 108 balls. Tim Seifert contributed 58, while Finn Allen scored 41. articles.title: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
articles.summary: Claims the entire Australian team knew of the 2018 sandpaper cheating plot are dividing the cricket world.
articles.body:
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.

Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.

"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."

A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.

Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."

"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.

There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.

"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.

"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."

Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.

In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.

"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."

However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.

David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.

But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.

And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.

Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".

"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.

"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."

He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.

He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.

"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.

Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.

"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."

"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.

"I don't know what the outcome will be."
